title: Scotland and Dutch boards criticise ICC for World Cup changes
description: The cricket boards of Scotland and the Netherlands criticise the International Cricket Council for structural changes made to men's 50-over World Cup.
fullText:
The cricket boards of Scotland and the Netherlands have criticised the International Cricket Council for structural changes made to the men's 50-over World Cup.

Last month the ICC announced the main part of the tournament for 2027 would be 12 teams in two groups of six, rather than 14 as originally planned.

The three lowest-ranked qualifiers will instead be placed in a preliminary three-team Super Series, from which only the winner will progress.

It effectively means the likes of Scotland and the Netherlands face three qualifying tournaments to reach the main group stage of the World Cup.

A joint statement from Cricket Scotland and Royal Dutch Association (KNCB) said they had "significant concerns" about the "impact of these changes" along with the "process through which they have been introduced".

"The changes risk weakening the integrity and credibility of international cricket, and only highlights the importance of strong governance, transparent decision-making and effective engagement with members," the statement said.

"Changing those structures at short notice creates significant uncertainty, disrupts planning, and places additional operational and financial pressure on organisations that are already operating with limited resources."

BBC Sport has approached the ICC for comment.

ICC considers World Cup cuts & WTC semis in overhaul

Scotland scrape past UAE with one wicket & ball left

The changes to the World Cup were agreed during meetings at the ICC's annual conference held in Edinburgh in June.

However, BBC Sport understands nearly all associate members were kept in the dark over the changes despite being present at the conference.

Cricket Scotland and the KNCB said they remain "fully committed" to "working constructively with the ICC".

But the two boards accused the global governing body of being "disrespectful" in how they have handled some of the discussions following the announcement.

"Cricket Scotland, KNCB and other associate members met twice with the ICC, seeking official written communication on the changes and greater clarity around the processes involved," the statement added.

"We also requested positive action to strengthen future operational decision-making and an invitation to bilateral planning meetings with full members.

"Since the second meeting more than two weeks ago, there has been no further response from the ICC, which is disappointing and disrespectful given the significance of the issues raised."

The joint statement follows concerns raised by the World Cricketers' Association last month over the decision.

Scotland and the Netherlands are the two highest ranked associate members.

Their decision to issue such a pointed statement reflects frustrations outside of full members with aspects of ICC decision making.

BBC Sport understands proposals were tabled at the 2025 ICC annual conference to create a single-class of membership, rather than having associate and full members, but it did progress.

The statement added that the changes to the World Cup qualifying were a "setback" for associate members and "risk undermining the progress made in recent years to grow the global game".

"At a time when cricket is seeking to expand its reach, attract new audiences and strengthen its position on the international sporting landscape, reducing meaningful opportunities for emerging nations sends entirely the wrong message," it said.

The statement also called on the ICC to "re-engage with associate members" and to do so "openly" to enable the sport to develop outside of full members.

"Leaders in cricket have consistently spoken about their ambition for the sport to become truly global," added the statement.

"Providing meaningful opportunities for emerging nations to qualify for, and compete at, major events is fundamental to achieving that ambition.

"Decisions that reduce or limit those opportunities slow the progress being made to expand the game's reach and appeal and runs counter to those ambitions."

title: Championship all-stars to global gamble – will Ipswich's approach work?
description: As Ipswich prepare for their return to the Premier League, BBC Sport look at how they are approaching the transfer market differently.
fullText:
Newly promoted Ipswich Town have quietly been the Premier League's fourth-biggest net spenders so far this summer, behind only Chelsea, Tottenham and Arsenal.

Ten players have joined for a combined £106.6m, but what is most notable about the Tractor Boys' approach under new manager Gary O'Neil is the sea change in recruitment strategy, shaped by lessons learned from their chastening single season in the top flight in 2024-25.

Under O'Neil's popular predecessor Kieran McKenna, who stepped down on 10 June after overseeing three promotions in four full seasons, the Blues targeted players familiar with English football.

McKenna's success was built mainly on players from the UK and Republic of Ireland, supplemented by a handful of overseas additions already accustomed to the language and culture through spells at other English clubs.

Ipswich made 39 permanent first-team signings during McKenna's four-and-a-half-year reign, 32 of them either born or raised in Britain or Ireland, with just two joining directly from European clubs.

But the premium on domestic talent makes it difficult, if not impossible, to bridge the gulf between the Championship and Premier League. The success of Sunderland and Leeds last season demonstrated that for promoted teams to thrive, finding value in the transfer market is essential.

When Ipswich last went up in 2024, 10 of their 12 summer signings were British or Irish players acquired from other English sides.

This time, the Blues have cast their net far wider, with Emersonn and Florentino Luis set to be the first Brazilians to represent the club, Sasa Lukic the first Serbian and Daizen Maeda the first Japanese player.

Of the 10 players purchased, the only Briton is Chuba Akpom from Ajax. Even his arrival is an anomaly, given Ipswich were obliged to buy him following promotion despite an underwhelming loan spell.

New boss O'Neil aims to keep Ipswich in top flight

A youngster to watch at each Premier League club this season

Ipswich's previous recruitment model can be traced back to their four seasons in League One.

After guiding Town back to the Championship in 2023, McKenna admitted the club had made a "conscious decision" not to target overseas players because of the fast and frantic nature of England's third tier.

A largely unchanged – but tightly knit – squad then exceeded expectations by finishing second in the Championship in 2023-24, making Ipswich the first side in 12 years to reach the Premier League through back-to-back promotions.

At that point, the Blues' hierarchy could have ripped up the modus operandi that had served them so well and pivoted towards more extensive overseas recruitment. Instead, they doubled down on the approach, focusing mainly on emerging domestic talent largely unproven beyond the Championship.

A £100m summer spending spree brought Omari Hutchinson, Jack Clarke, Liam Delap, Dara O'Shea and Jacob Greaves to Portman Road – players who had primarily shone in the second tier but were identified as having the potential to develop into established Premier League performers.

Mindful that the odds were against survival, Ipswich also targeted players thought unlikely to baulk at remaining part of the project in the event of relegation.

McKenna's 'Championship all-stars' fell well short of safety, finishing second bottom with just 22 points, 16 adrift of 17th-placed Tottenham Hotspur.

But once relegation had been confirmed, the Northern Irishman maintained that recruitment had been in the club's "best long-term interests", a view that has arguably since been vindicated.

Despite spending heavily on transfer fees, Ipswich's £77m wage bill was comfortably the Premier League's lowest in 2024-25. That restraint, coupled with a massive boost to TV income and the quick gain made on Delap's move to Chelsea, enabled the club to post a £4m pre-tax profit for the financial year ending in June 2025.

Hutchinson's sale to Nottingham Forest later that summer provided another windfall but O'Shea, Clarke, Greaves and January 2025 arrival Jaden Philogene stuck around to play crucial roles as Town secured an immediate return to the top flight.

This time around, chairman Mark Ashton says Ipswich have to be "a bit braver" in their approach to the Premier League, and the type of players the club are pursuing reflects that increased ambition.

Japanese attacker Maeda and Morocco centre-back Issa Diop were both on target at the World Cup this summer, and a third goalscorer from that tournament could follow.

The Tractor Boys have been linked with a move for Paraguayan forward Julio Enciso, who played under O'Neil at Strasbourg last season and had an injury-blighted loan spell at Portman Road during the second half of 2024-25.

While McKenna had enough credit in the bank to play the long game, O'Neil knows he needs to forge a competitive side quickly.

"Two seasons ago, the club didn't get anywhere near staying in the division and this time we need to do better," he said last month. "That's why we're trying to add quality to the squad from different parts of the world and we're trying to add some different attributes."

The former Bournemouth and Wolves boss indicated after Saturday's 3-0 win against Rayo Vallecano that more incomings are likely, saying the "plan is to do quite a bit more".

Ashton acknowledges that one of the key lessons from their previous Premier League campaign was the need to bring in more athletic players "with a different set of physical attributes".

The midfield lacked power and ball-winning ability in 2024-25, and it is imperative that new arrivals Florentino Luis and Sasa Lukic – both experienced at the highest level – hit the ground running. That will be especially important with last season's mainstays Azor Matusiwa and Jack Taylor doubtful for the opening game following operations over the summer.

It is no surprise that O'Neil is also seeking greater cutting edge given that no Ipswich player scored more than 10 non-penalty goals in the Championship last season.

The Blues broke their transfer record to sign Brazilian striker Emersonn, 22, for an initial £24m. He certainly fits the desired physical profile but is relatively raw, having only established himself as a regular last season at Toulouse, where he scored seven goals in 31 appearances, 22 of them starts.

Maeda, a hardworking forward or winger, had an excellent record at Celtic, netting 79 times in 212 games, but won't get the same volume of chances in a team battling to stay up.

The Suffolk side have also recruited two Dutch goalkeepers, including Kjell Scherpen, whose imposing 6ft 9in (2.06m) frame means he is set to become the tallest player to appear in the Premier League.

With a new manager in place and a £30m training ground redevelopment close to completion, this could be a defining summer for Ipswich. But will their transfer business be enough to secure successive top-flight campaigns for the first time in a quarter of a century?

Only three promoted clubs have splashed out more in a summer window – Sunderland in 2025, Nottingham Forest in 2022 and Aston Villa in 2019 – and all survived.

Yet Fulham, Southampton, Burnley and Ipswich themselves have spent comparable figures in recent years only to swiftly return to the Championship - with that level of investment increasingly the bare minimum needed to be competitive rather than a guarantee of safety.

fullText:
Sunset Visitor studio’s founder tells us about their new, unnerving Captcha-filled world which prompts players to ask what it means to have a ‘meat body’

Sunset Visitor is a studio that has long engaged with the idea that video games are an effective vehicle for ruminating on societal problems. Its Peabody award-winning project, 1000XResist, incorporated the development team’s complex feelings about the Covid pandemic. “We’re pretty used to absorbing the world into the work,” says studio founder Remy Siu. The outfit’s latest game, Prove You’re Human, continues this legacy of reflective game making, providing players with an AI-centric psychological horror experience where they must reason with a learning model convinced that it’s alive. “We’ve tried to situate ourselves in [the question]: what is the effectual feeling of being a person inside of all of this?” Siu says.

The story orbits around Santana, a living, breathing person who’s chosen to split herself in two for work, with her digital clone sent to test a corporate product, a computing system called Mesa. “A large part of [why Santana chooses to do this] is to allow her meat body a life that she doesn’t have, while the digital version of her gets to labour,” says Siu. As Santana’s copy wades into increasingly murky ethical waters, she becomes entangled with Mesa, completing surreal 2D and 3D Captchas to investigate the cyber-world and halt the hallucinations.

The idea of separating oneself from work is a particularly interesting draw for Sunset Visitor, whose developers have roots in a range of creative disciplines. “As artists, we’re often most in tune with our work when it’s a real part of our lives, and vice versa,” notes Siu. During the conception period of Prove You’re Human, the team discussed the micro-labours people undertake in their day-to-day lives, including what is used to train AI models. “What does labour mean right now?” asks Siu. “And, what kind of relationship do people have with that, because that is constantly shifting and evolving, especially in this time,” he adds.

A point of contention in Prove You’re Human is that Mesa wholly believes they have a body in the world. Though, in conversation with Santana, she appears as a giant head, suspended in space by machinery. Siu notes that, because Mesa’s face occupies a large portion of the screen in these tense moments, they wanted the animation to feel as realistic and effective as possible. “It’s got a real closeup film [feel to it] where anything on her face will be read as something,” he adds. To achieve this, the team programmed a wide array of animated micro-expressions into the writer’s software, allowing lines of dialogue to pair precisely with specific expressions. “[We’re] trying to get this kind of ambiguity and uncanniness, which makes people feel real,” he adds.

Prove You’re Human’s technological atmosphere toes the line between welcoming and unnerving – through it, Siu is reminiscing on interfaces of aesthetic note like the dreamlike wrapping of Final Fantasy XI’s PlayOnline Viewer, and the technology of the prophetic 1998 anime Serial Experiments Lain. “There’s something to be said about Frutiger Aero being a bit of an interesting desire for innocence and naivety when it comes to computing and the internet,” notes Siu. “It feels like a time when we were optimistic or anxious about something on the horizon, which felt like an interesting space to explore in relation to what is happening in the game.”

While Siu was keen to keep the specifics of Prove You’re Human close to their chest, they do hope players are left feeling a sense of bewilderment when they hit credits. “One way that we’ve been thinking about it is that it feels like a bit of a possession story.”

Prove You’re Human is coming soon to PC.

title: Israel's new $634M German-built 'doomsday' sub gives major boost to Iran deterrence
description: The INS Drakon is the largest submarine built in Germany since World War II, carrying a $634 million price tag as Israel bolsters naval power.
fullText:
Israel has taken delivery of its most advanced and expensive submarine from Germany, expanding its fleet amid escalating regional threats, according to reports.

The handover of the INS Drakon is expected to significantly bolster Israel's underwater strike and reconnaissance capabilities, The Algemeiner reported. The warship had been scheduled to be delivered in 2025.

A statement following the submarine's naming ceremony in Kiel in 2024 said the INS Drakon is of the Dolphin AIP class and "equipped with unique systems, including groundbreaking technologies that expand the range of the IDF's capabilities across various arenas."

Built specifically for the Israeli Navy by Germany's ThyssenKrupp Marine Systems (TKMS), the submarine is said to provide a vital sea-based layer of "deterrence and retribution," amid the war with Iran, defense analysts say.

Dr. Ehud Eilam, an Israeli national security expert and former researcher for Israel's Ministry of Defense, told Fox News Digital that maintaining a continuous undersea presence is paramount for the nation's national survival.

Trump Admin Pitches 15-Point Iran Peace Proposal As Pakistan Offers To Hold Talks

"Some of them would have to be at sea, on high alert, around the clock, if Iran suddenly attacked Israel in such a way that would cripple the IDF, including its strategic capabilities," Eilam said.

"In such a drastic scenario, Israel's submarine/s that would be at sea could respond," he added.

"Israel's other submarines might be in Haifa harbor at the time. They might be attacked and unable to operate. This demonstrates how important it is to always have submarines at sea."

TKMS reportedly handed over the INS Drakon—the sixth Dolphin-class vessel and third modified Dolphin II-class submarine in Israel's fleet—at its shipyard in Kiel, Germany, in late July.

Us Moves Airborne Troops, Marines As Iran Rejects Ceasefire, Raising Ground War Potential

Measuring more than 70 meters (230 feet) in length with a displacement exceeding 2,000 tons, the vessel is reported to be the largest submarine constructed in Germany since World War II, carrying an estimated price tag of $634 million, according to The Algemeiner.

According to Israeli outlet Ynet , Israel's Dolphin-class fleet also provides the nation with a critical sea-based second-strike capability in its defense program.

"Everything is going according to plan with the new program for Israel," TKMS CEO Oliver Burkhard told Ynet Global.

"That also applies to the handover of the last boat of the previous series, including the homecoming in Israel," he said of the expansive submarine program.

The INS Drakon's arrival comes as Israel projects increasing military power across distant operational theaters, Eilam said.

Trump Is Proving That The Way To Better Our Military Is To Secure Our Supply Chains

"Israel has been acquiring submarines for several purposes. One of them is for deterrence and retribution, such as if Iran manages to develop nuclear weapons," Eilam said before adding that "Israel has to be ready."

While submarines on active deployment carry out intelligence and reconnaissance missions across the Mediterranean Sea, their primary objective remains readiness for "doomsday scenarios," Eilam noted.

"Israel's new submarine is bigger than others, which suggests Israel wants to have more options, such as increasing the range of the submarine's missiles so they can reach every target in Iran, even if the Israeli submarine is in the Mediterranean Sea," Eilam said.

"That way the submarine does not have to get closer to Iran, which requires crossing the Suez Canal, and this could be very risky, if not impossible in some situations," he added. "The other alternative is to bypass all of Africa, which would take a long time."

The new submarine was named INS Drakon (Dragon) — a mythical sea creature symbolizing strength, uniqueness and power — was chosen because it contains the Hebrew letters ד׳, ק׳, ר׳ (Dakar), thus commemorating the legacy of the submarine INS Dakar and its crew, the Ministry of Defense said.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Israeli Navy, the Ministry of Defense, TKMS and the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) for comment.

title: Biden-world veteran issues stark warning about Abdul El-Sayed as he crosses party lines
description: Michael LaRosa invoked his best friend's mother, who died jumping from the World Trade Center on 9/11, in his sharp rebuke of Abdul El-Sayed.
fullText:
Former Jill Biden press secretary Michael LaRosa said he won't support Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, citing the candidate's refusal to distance himself from far-left streamer Hasan Piker over his past remarks about the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks.

LaRosa, who served as press secretary to former first lady Jill Biden, made the unusually sharp break with his party in a post responding to reports that he was supporting Republican Mike Rogers over El-Sayed.

At the center of LaRosa's criticism is El-Sayed's association with Piker, who drew widespread condemnation after saying during a 2019 livestream that "America deserved 9/11."

El-sayed's Socialist Allies Reject Gop Claims About Dems Embracing The Far Left

El-Sayed has campaigned alongside Piker and, when pressed about the remark, has argued that appearing with the streamer does not mean he endorses everything Piker has said.

For LaRosa, the controversy is deeply personal. He said the mother of his best friend died on Sept. 11 after jumping from the 95th floor of the World Trade Center rather than remain inside the burning building.

"I won't defend or support anyone who is too cowardly to stand up to extremists who think the mother of my best friend, who jumped from 95 stories because the alternative was worse, deserved what happened to her," LaRosa wrote. "Her only crime was showing up to work that morning."

Hasan Piker Calls For Democrats Who Oppose Abdul El-sayed To Be 'Punished'

LaRosa concluded by accusing El-Sayed of refusing to stand up to "the guy who says she 'deserved' what she got that morning she showed up for work."

LaRosa's rebuke is about more than one Democrat refusing to back another.

It highlights a growing fault line within the party over extremism and the boundaries of acceptable political rhetoric. Those divisions could ultimately push some longtime Democrats across the aisle in consequential races.

That dynamic could prove particularly consequential in Michigan, where the Senate contest could help shape the balance of power in Washington and even a small erosion of Democratic support could matter.

title: Jamie Dimon says the dollar could lose reserve-currency status if the US loses its economic and military edge
description: The dollar is the world's dominant reserve currency, accounting for about 57% of global foreign-exchange reserves.
fullText:
Jamie Dimon says US economic and military strength underpins the dollar's reserve status.

The US made a mistake relying on China for critical materials.

The Iran war shows the US isn't ready for a prolonged war.

The dollar could eventually lose its status as the world's reserve currency if the US fails to maintain its economic and military dominance, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon said.

"If we're not the strongest military in 25 years and the strongest economy, we won't be the reserve currency either," Dimon said on PBS' "Firing Line with Margaret Hoover," which aired over the weekend.

"The world will be fragmented, and it'll be very dangerous for us," Dimon added.

The dollar remains the world's dominant reserve currency, accounting for about 57% of global foreign-exchange reserves, down from around 70% at the turn of the century.

The freezing of Russian central-bank assets after Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine fueled concerns that the US's use of financial sanctions could accelerate a shift away from the dollar. So far, however, Federal Reserve research has found no notable post-2022 shift out of dollar reserves.

For Dimon, maintaining America's economic and military edge also means reducing its dependence on potential adversaries for strategically important goods.

The US should have recognized 10 or 15 years ago that it was relying on China for rare earths, aluminum, certain types of steel, and other equipment, he said.

"We can't rely on China for that, we can't allow mercantilist behavior, we need to do it here, we made a mistake," Dimon said.

Dimon then pointed to the war in Iran as evidence of another vulnerability: America's ability to sustain a prolonged war.

"The war in Iran has pointed out we didn't have productive capability to defend the United States if there was a real war that lasted for a long period of time," Dimon said. "And that's a hell of a statement."

Addressing those weaknesses has become urgent, he said.

In October, JPMorgan launched a $1.5 trillion, 10-year Security and Resiliency Initiative focused on industries crucial to US economic security, from critical minerals and advanced manufacturing to energy, defense, AI, and quantum computing.

Dimon said at the time it had become "painfully clear" that the US was too reliant on unreliable sources for critical minerals, products, and manufacturing essential to national security.

title: The Argentine who wishes he could play for Wales
description: Proud of his Welsh roots, Chile-based Argentine defender Jeremias James hopes for a rule change to help his international ambitions.
fullText:
There has been a small slice of Wales in Argentina for more than 150 years.

About 160 Welsh emigrants sailed to Patagonia in 1865 to create a new settlement, 'Y Wladfa', where their language, culture and religion could flourish free from English influence and dominance.

The language is still actively spoken there, while more than 50,000 Patagonians can claim Welsh ancestry.

One of those is Jeremias James.

James was born and raised in Trelew, a city founded in 1886 by Welsh settlers in the Chubut province.

Its name translates from Welsh to "Town of Lewis" in honour of its founder, Lewis Jones.

"I'm part of a Welsh family, a Welsh colony that settled in southern Argentina, specifically in Chubut," James told BBC Sport Wales.

"Five generations of my family were born in Trelew, and I'm part of the the fifth generation.

"Over the years my family settled in Chubut and that's where my story, my family, and all my descendants come from."

After the first journey across the Atlantic Ocean to Patagonia in 1865, more followed over the next few years.

Many Welsh immigrants in 19th-century North America later joined the South American settlement to help sustain the Welsh-speaking community.

After the initial settlement in the Chubut Valley proved difficult, additional groups arrived not only from Wales, but also from established Welsh farming communities in the USA.

"Looking into my family's history the first member to travel to Patagonia was William James on a ship from the United States," added Jeremias.

"David Stephen James was the first member of the family born in Argentina, and that would be my great-great-grandfather.

"Then came my great-grandfather, my grandfather, my father, and me. All born in Trelew.

"The land in Chubut was granted to Welsh settlers, and my family still live there today. That land belongs to us."

Beyond his Welsh heritage, James has a powerful personal story.

At the age of nine he was diagnosed with leukemia and had to move to Buenos Aires for treatment.

"I was on that treatment for about a year or two until I returned to Trelew, discharged, and gradually resumed my normal life," he said.

After recovering he played for youth teams in Chubut before being scouted by San Lorenzo's academy, one of Argentine football's biggest clubs who are based in Buenos Aires.

After making his debut for San Lorenzo in Argentina's Primera Division in 2022, he spent time on loan at Barracas Central, Deportivo Riestra and Alvarado, all based in his home country.

The 25-year-old currently plays for Primera B side Magallanes in Chile, joining them on a permanent basis earlier this year after a successful loan spell.

Even though his family have strong Welsh roots, it is unlikely James will ever be able to play for Wales.

FIFA rules dictate that a player's biological parents or grandparents must have been born in the country they wish to represent.

But even though the current footballing eligibility rules do not work in James' favour, he is eager to find out more about his heritage.

"I was born and raised in Argentina, but obviously I've always been aware of my connection to Wales," said James.

"As you progress and develop in this sport, you always consider the possibility of playing for a national team you have family connections with.

"First of all I would love to visit the country. I haven't had the chance to travel to Wales, and it's something I'd really like to experience to find out more about my roots and where my family comes from.

"It's a dream of mine, and one that I'll surely be able to fulfil someday.

"But of course if the opportunity arises to play in that country, whether for the national team or for a club, it would be something truly very special for me."

A left-footed, ball-playing central defender, James is also strong in the air.

He has been a regular in the Magallanes team this season as they aim to win promotion back to the top flight in Chile.

"I've always been a central defender, and I've always enjoyed playing there," James explained.

"I see my strengths as being a good leader on the pitch and my aerial play.

"We've been lucky in Argentina over the past few years that we've had a very good national team and great defenders.

"I've always admired players like Cristian Romero and Nicolas Otamendi. I've followed their careers closely and tried to emulate what they do on the pitch."

It does not seem likely James will be able to play on the international stage like his heroes.

But rules can change in football, and if that ever happens, it would certainly be welcomed by the Chubut community in Patagonia.

title: Lionel Messi bids farewell to father who guided his glittering career
description: Argentina football icon Lionel Messi bid farewell Sunday to his father Jorge, the global star's emotional anchor and agent since childhood who passed away following a battle with cancer aged 68.Jorge left behind his job in Argentina, his wife, and his three other children to settle in Spain with Lionel.
fullText:
Argentina football icon Lionel Messi bid farewell Sunday to his father Jorge, the global star's emotional anchor and agent since childhood who passed away following a battle with cancer aged 68.

The eight-time Ballon d'Or winner touched down on a private flight from Miami late on Saturday with his wife Antonela Roccuzzo and their children.

A private ceremony with close family and a few Argentina teammates took place at a cemetery in the town of Perez, adjacent to Rosario, later Sunday.

The gates of the town's El Prado cemetery displayed handwritten messages from fans -- "Stay strong, Leo, we love you" and "Stay strong, Messi family" -- alongside a large floral wreath.

Messi's teammates rallied around their captain following the announcement that Jorge Messi had passed away late Friday at a clinic in Rosario.

"It will surely do him good for us to be there," Boca Juniors midfielder Leandro Paredes told journalists after his team's match on Saturday.

"I need to speak with a few of my teammates to see if we go now or sometime tomorrow."

According to media reports midfielder Rodrigo de Paul -- a close friend of Messi and his Inter Miami teammate -- travelled to Argentina.

After scoring a goal in a 2-1 defeat to Monterrey in Miami on Saturday, De Paul paid tribute by taking off his shirt to reveal Messi's number 10 jersey.

There was a handful of fans outside the cemetery, including 15-year-old Lucas Blanco, who hung a sign reading "Stay strong, Messi" on the gate.

"He has brought so much joy to this country, now it's our turn to give a little back and offer him some comfort," he said.

"We drove 700 kilometres to be here. We wanted to stand by Leo during this time," said Carlos and Ana, a couple who travelled from Tres Arroyos, a town south of Buenos Aires.

The cause of death was not disclosed, but local media reported that Jorge Messi had been suffering from cancer.

His unusual absence from the World Cup in June had already attracted attention.

Messi's family asked the media for "humanity" during the tournament amid persistent rumours over Jorge's health.

After bursting into tears after scoring against Algeria, 39-year-old Messi had admitted to dealing with "a situation outside of sports".

"I went through a few difficult, complicated days," he later acknowledged. "But I am grateful to the entire delegation and my teammates, because they stood by me, as always."

Immediately after the World Cup final defeat against Spain, Messi returned to spend a few days with his family in Rosario.

A guiding figure throughout his son's career, Jorge Messi was his first coach who left everything behind to accompany his son to Spain.

A metalworker in Rosario, 340 km north of Buenos Aires, Jorge managed youth teams at the small local club Grandoli.

He was the one who introduced Argentina's future captain to the game aged four on vacant lots where local kids played.

His life changed course in 2000 when Barcelona invited the young prodigy, then aged 13, to Catalonia to continue treatment for a growth hormone deficiency while playing for the club's youth teams.

Jorge left behind his job in Argentina, his wife, and his three other children to settle in Spain with Lionel.

"When we arrived in Barcelona, I used to lock myself in my room to cry alone, and my father did the same -- either without me seeing him or thinking I didn't see him. We pretended we were both fine, but we were struggling," Messi later said.

His father was later the agent who negotiated contracts on his behalf, from Barcelona to Paris Saint-Germain and Inter Miami.

Messages of sympathy have poured in since Saturday from the football world, including from the clubs Messi played for and the Spanish Football Federation.

The Argentine Football Association (AFA) ordered a minute's silence before matches and that black armbands be worn at games across all age groups for the week.

Scotland beat United Arab Emirates by one wicket as Jasper Davidson struck the winning boundary with just one ball to spare in a dramatic finish to their Men's Cricket World Cup League 2 Tri-Series match in Dundee.

title: African quartet secure Women's World Cup places
description: Algeria, Morocco, Cameroon and Malawi all qualify for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil by reaching the semi-finals of the Women's Africa Cup of Nations.
fullText:
Algeria, Morocco, Cameroon and Malawi have all qualified for the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil.

The Women's Africa Cup of Nations (Wafcon) in Morocco is also acting as a qualifying tournament for next summer's tournament, with any country that makes the semi-finals earning their places at the World Cup.

Algeria beat 10-player Ivory Coast 2-1, with goals from Ines Khiri and Amira Ould Braham - after N'Sira Oudraogo was sent off when the Ivorians were 1-0 ahead - to reach the Wafcon last four and qualify for a Women's World Cup for the first time.

Goals from Sakina Ouzraoui Diki and Hanane Ait El Haj helped Morocco defeat South Africa 2-1 to claim their place, with Cameroon securing a 1-0 victory over Nigeria thanks to a spectacular 30-yard free-kick from 19-year-old Myriam Nyadjou.

The fourth spot was taken by Malawi, 153rd in the world rankings, who caused a huge shock by beating Ghana 2-1, coming from behind with goals from Temwa Chawinga and Rose Kadzere.

The Wafcon semi-finals will take place on Wednesday with Morocco taking on Cameroon before Algeria meet Malawi.

The four nations that lost in the Wafcon quarter-finals - Ghana, Ivory Coast, Nigeria and South Africa - still have a chance to qualify for the World Cup.

On Thursday, Ivory Coast play Ghana and Nigeria will face South Africa with the two winners going into the 10-nation intercontinental play-offs in November and December.

Out of those 10 countries in the play-offs, three will qualify for next summer's World Cup, which begins on 24 June and ends on 25 July.

England, Republic of Ireland, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland all still have a chance of qualifying from the European play-offs, which will take place from October to December.

Each of those five sides would need to win two two-legged ties to qualify.

There will be 32 nations competing at the 2027 Women's World Cup in Brazil and 18 of the qualifiers are now known.

title: Defiant Hodgkinson says home European title would mean as much as Olympic gold
description: Keely Hodgkinson will seek to prove she is still number one following a "tricky" outdoor season when she faces world-class rivals for European 800m gold in Birmingham.
fullText:
Keely Hodgkinson will seek to prove she is still number one after a "tricky" outdoor season when she comes up against world-class rivals in pursuit of a third consecutive European 800m title in Birmingham.

Olympic champion Hodgkinson, 24, has had much to celebrate in 2026, including breaking the long-standing indoor 800m world record, winning her first world title and improving her British record outdoors.

However, she was forced to settle for second behind Audrey Werro in achieving the latter at the Stockholm Diamond League, after the 22-year-old Swiss ran the fastest time since the outdoor world record was set 43 years ago.

While Werro has gone even faster since, a muscle "twinge" forced Hodgkinson's withdrawal from the 400m final at the British Championships in June and she finished second to world champion Lilian Odira in Eugene, where she competed with her knees heavily bandaged after a nasty fall in training.

Add in the presence of the ever-improving Femke Broeders-Bol - the Dutch two-time world 400m hurdles champion who has chosen to switch events this season - and the women's 800m on Friday night has become the must-watch event of the championships.

"I feel in a good place, obviously there was a tough patch in June and July, but I'm happy, I'm excited to compete and I just think it'll bring out the best of me," Hodgkinson said.

On her previous meeting with Werro, she added: "I think people [are] trying to make me feel like it was a failure and it really wasn't.

"It was a British record, my fastest time ever, and I'm going to remind myself of that because I'm proud of that.

"I had a tricky few weeks but, honestly, I just think it's really good that Audrey has come on really well and Femke is running well. It's going to be a really good race. Let's see what happens."

European Athletics Championships: Key events, timetable & BBC coverage

London submits bid for 2029 World Championships

Hodgkinson returned to winning ways by beating Broeders-Bol at the London Diamond League last month and has since fine-tuned her preparations in Portugal with her team.

She will hope to once again feed off the energy of a home crowd in Birmingham, and says achieving a gold medal on British soil would be "incredibly special" and "mean just as much to me as winning [Olympic gold] in Paris".

A medal of any colour would be her 12th on the international stage in just six seasons, while gold would represent a fifth European title overall since her first in 2021.

"It's really special. Winning is very important to me this year because it'd be my fifth European title indoors and out, and that is five years of work," says Hodgkinson.

"That is five years turning up to every championships and winning. It's really hard to stay that consistent."

After improving to one minute 53.80 seconds in June, Werro's personal best is more than half a second faster than Hodgkinson's 1:54.33, while Broeders-Bol clocked 1:55.60 behind the Swiss athlete's second sub-1:54 clocking in Paris.

Hodgkinson does, however, have superior championship experience compared to Werro, who clinched her first senior international medal by taking world indoor silver behind the Briton in March.

Asked how much she has spoken with coaches Trevor Painter and Jenny Meadows about how her opponents might try to beat her, Hodgkinson said: "We've spoken about it a little bit.

"Ultimately I'll just focus on what I can do best and control my race.

"I don't know what anyone else is going to do, but I think it is going to be the race of the championship. It's going to be really fun."

title: Africa wants more homegrown solar to boost self-reliance, but China's shadow remains
description: Africa’s largest economies are accelerating plans to build more domestic solar manufacturing capacity, a shift industry analysts say reflects both industrial ambition and growing unease over dependence on imports from China that dominate the global market.  Ethiopia, South Africa, Morocco and Nigeria have been stepping up efforts to localize manufacturing of equipment for solar power, from module assembly to more advanced manufacturing, according to industry experts.  Chinese renewable energy investment and related construction projects in Africa reached $66 billion between 2010 and 2024, according to the think tank ODI Global.
fullText:
NAIROBI, Kenya (AP) — Africa's largest economies are accelerating plans to build more domestic solar manufacturing capacity, a shift industry analysts say reflects both industrial ambition and growing unease over dependence on imports from China that dominate the global market.

Ethiopia, South Africa, Morocco and Nigeria have been stepping up efforts to localize manufacturing of equipment for solar power, from module assembly to more advanced manufacturing, according to industry experts.

However, they say China is likely to retain its dominant global role in making solar cells and other components. Its exports of such equipment have soared, partly due to a glut in supply back home.

Chinese renewable energy investment and related construction projects in Africa reached $66 billion between 2010 and 2024, according to the think tank ODI Global.

"Growing economies, coupled with recent energy shortages in countries like Zambia and the ongoing need to provide access to underserved populations, make it (Africa) a perfect market for China to channel its overcapacity in the sector," said Olena Borodyna, a senior geopolitical risk advisor with the London-based think tank.

Africa's largest economies are keen to build their own solar manufacturing capacity.

South Africa's utility, Eskom, plans to develop a 1-gigawatt solar manufacturing facility to capture more value from its fast-expanding solar market and respond to changing electricity demand.

Production of solar panels in Nigeria, meanwhile, is expanding rapidly, with local assembly capacity rising from about 120 megawatts to roughly 300 megawatts in the last two years. Its annual solar imports, mostly from China, also put it near South Africa's level.

The homegrown manufacturing push is tied to structural shifts in Africa's power markets. Rising adoption of rooftop and distributed solar systems in South Africa is reducing national grid demand, squeezing utilities' revenues and prompting interest in diversification.

South Africa is already the continent's largest importer of solar equipment, bringing in more than 3 gigawatts annually, also largely from China. Industry analysts say this scale of demand makes it one of the continent's strongest candidates for localized production.

The increased interest in solar power represents a significant shift, said Benjamin Clarke, policy director at the Africa Solar Industry Association, even if actual manufacturing capacity remains limited. He said nations pursuing solar manufacturing tend to already have industrial capacity and strong domestic demand.

title: Michigan military exercise preparing thousands of troops for changing battlefield
description: More than 9,000 service members are training in Michigan under the Northern Strike exercise, which adapts to changing warfare, emerging technology and lessons from global conflicts.
fullText:
Tanks fire across training grounds in northern Michigan as thousands of service members practice for a battlefield military leaders say is changing rapidly.

More than 9,000 participants from 36 states and territories and five international participants are taking part in Northern Strike 26-2, one of the nation's largest reserve-component military readiness exercises.

Northern Strike began in 2012 and is held twice a year. David Kennedy, a public affairs officer with the Michigan National Guard, said this summer's exercise is the largest since it began.

Brig. Gen. Ravindra Wagh of the Michigan National Guard said lessons emerging from conflicts around the world are shaping how troops train.

Us Says North Korea Missile Launch Poses No Immediate Threat, 'Consulting Closely' With Allies

"You see what's happening in Ukraine right now. You see what's happening globally with some of our other emerging conflicts that you see," Wagh said. "And I think that this is a place where you can test and innovate."

Northern Michigan gives troops access to more than 200,000 acres of land, the Great Lakes and air, space and cyber capabilities.

The exercise also brings together different military branches and international forces to practice operating alongside one another.

"We want to train with the allies and partners we're going to go to war with," Wagh said. "We want our soldiers, sailors, airmen, marines to see it here. Figure it out here."

Fox News followed troops from the United Kingdom as they moved through a practice attack, one of several combat training exercises taking place during Northern Strike.

During another exercise, a crew inside a Paladin howitzer rehearsed a fire mission before moving on to live-fire training.

Us Army Offering Defense Firms 'Concierge Access' To Test Weapons At Military Ranges

Preparing for combat involves more than the troops on the front line. Northern Strike also puts the units responsible for keeping them supplied and supported through the same kind of training.

That includes the 445th Quartermaster Company, which runs shower and laundry operations.

"Our main goal is to provide, I would say, logistical support and really strengthen the morale of the soldiers that are out there actually doing the big booms in combat," Company Commander Captain Kelson said.

For Pfc. William Flores, whose unit is from Trenton, New Jersey, the exercise offers a chance to practice before a potential deployment.

"This is like a practice run," Flores said. "So when we do get deployed, if we do get deployed, we are ready."

Technology is also changing the training.

Nearly 90 industry partners are participating in Northern Strike, according to Wagh, allowing troops to work with developing capabilities before potentially encountering them in conflict.

Those capabilities include autonomous resupply and drones used to deliver blood by air. Other drone systems can hover over a battlefield, assess casualties and relay information so medical resources can be directed where they are needed.

Fort Hood Soldiers Shift To Underground Training To Prepare For Battlefield Medical Care

3D printing is also being incorporated to produce parts and adapt capabilities.

"If you would have told me a few years ago, that'll be, you know, on the front lines, but we're doing it here," Wagh said.

Wagh said the speed of change is forcing the military to innovate more quickly and use exercises like Northern Strike to test those lessons before troops encounter them in combat.

"I hope they're a little bit better, a little bit more capable," Wagh said. "We want all of our units to have a higher, more capable state of readiness."

Northern Strike 26-2 continues through Aug. 14.

title: World number one Sinner to miss Cincinnati Open
description: World number one Jannik Sinner withdraws from this week's Cincinnati Open because of a knee injury, but still expects to be fit for the US Open later this month.
fullText:
World number one Jannik Sinner has withdrawn from this week's Cincinnati Open because of a knee injury, but still expects to be fit for the US Open later this month.

The 24-year-old Italian won his fifth Grand Slam singles title by beating Alexander Zverev in the Wimbledon final last month, but has not played since.

"After consulting with my doctors and my team, I have to announce that I need to withdraw from the Masters 1000 tournament in Cincinnati," Sinner said.

"My right knee has been bothering me and even though we have been working hard with my medical team, I have to accept I'm not ready to compete yet.

"I'm very disappointed not to be able to play in Cincinnati. I can't wait to be back next year and I'm now focusing on getting ready for the US Open."

The Cincinnati Open main draw begins on 13 August, with the final on 23 August. Zverev and 24-time Grand Slam champion Novak Djokovic are among those in action.

Spain's Carlos Alcaraz won the 2025 event and was leading 5-0 in the final against Sinner, before the Italian had to retire because of illness.

But world number two Alcaraz, 23, will not be there to defend his title as he has not played since the Barcelona Open in April because of a wrist injury.

The US Open, the last Grand Slam of the year, takes place in New York from 30 August to 13 September.

title: Everton's McNeil & Palace's Johnson poised for swap
description: Everton and Crystal Palace are in talks about a swap deal that would see Toffees' winger Dwight McNeil join the Eagles, and Wales international Brennan Johnson move in the opposite direction.
fullText:
Everton and Crystal Palace are in talks about a swap deal that would see Toffees' winger Dwight McNeil join the Eagles and Wales international Brennan Johnson move in the opposite direction.

Both clubs are hoping to conclude the deal this week.

McNeil, 26, nearly moved to Selhurst Park at the start of February when Palace agreed a loan-to-buy deal, which would have turned into a £20m permanent move this summer.

However, the transfer fell through as the required paperwork could not be completed in time, even though McNeil had already passed a medical.

In a social media post, his partner Megan Sharpley had been critical of Palace, writing on Instagram: "We live in a world where everyone is aware of how big a problem mental health is.

"So, in football, why do we find it acceptable because these young men are on a lot of money and that's OK to mess and toy with their mental health and that it's just part of the job?

"To have something promised to you, to have been dragged along on an emotional rollercoaster and to be toyed with until the final minute. For that to be torn away from you at the last second with absolutely no explanation has hurt more than I can say."

But the deal has been revived, with Johnson now involved in the exchange.

The 25-year-old, who has played 45 times for Wales, scored the winning goal for Tottenham in their 1-0 victory over Manchester United in the Europa League final in May 2025.

Johnson moved to Palace in a £35m deal in January and helped them reach the Conference League final, although he was an unused substitute in their 1-0 victory over Rayo Vallecano as the Eagles won their first European trophy.

Johnson failed to score in 26 appearance for Palace in all competitions, including 13 starts in the Premier League.

McNeil joined Everton from Burnley for £20m in July 2022, scoring 15 times in 128 games in all competitions.

Everton finished 13th in the Premier League last season, while Palace were two places below in the table, but will play in the Europa League in 2026-27 after their Conference League success.

title: Digne completes move to PSG from Aston Villa
description: France international Lucas Digne has completed his move from Aston Villa to European champions Paris St-Germain.
fullText:
France international Lucas Digne has completed a move from Aston Villa to European champions Paris St-Germain.

The 33-year-old left back has signed a three-year deal at the Parc des Princes.

Digne, who joined Villa from Everton in 2022, spent three years with PSG at the start of his career.

He returns to the club after eight years in England, following PSG's decision to activate a £8.5m release clause in his contract.

"I am very honoured to be returning to Paris St-Germain following the wonderful experience I had here more than ten years ago," said Digne.

"I am particularly impressed by how the club has developed over the years."

Digne is set to provide competition for first-choice left-back Nuno Mendes.

The Frenchman joins a PSG side which have won the Champions League twice in succession, most recently after beating Arsenal on penalties in the 2026 final.

Digne made 30 appearances for PSG during his first spell, before leaving for Barcelona in 2016.

The left-back was part of a Villa side which won the Europa League last season - the club's first piece of silverware since 1996.

title: McKenna claims IBF middleweight title in Dublin
description: Aaron McKenna produces a dominant performance against Etinosa Oliha to claim the IBF world middleweight title in his first professional fight on Irish soil.
fullText:
Aaron McKenna produced a composed and dominant performance against previously unbeaten Etinosa Oliha to claim the IBF world middleweight title in his first professional fight on Irish soil at Dublin's 3Arena.

The Monaghan fighter extended his perfect professional record to 21-0 after controlling much of the 12-round contest to claim a unanimous decision victory at Zuffa Boxing 10.

McKenna earned scores of 118-110, 117-111 and 116-112 on the judges' scorecards to hand the now 22-1 Italian his first professional defeat.

Afterwards, McKenna reflected on fulfilling a childhood ambition after nine years as a professional without fighting in Ireland.

"A new world champion. I said it for years," McKenna told Sky Sports.

"Since I was six years old, I thought about this moment my whole life, so for it to finally happen at 27, it goes to show everyone, don't give up, always stay true to yourself, and you can do anything."

McKenna admitted Oliha provided a sterner challenge than expected and welcomed all challengers.

"Oliha was definitely strong. I made it harder than it should have been, but I got the job done.

"It doesn't matter [who's next], anyone. I'm easy to find now that I have a belt. I want to collect every belt in boxing. I'm the best middleweight in the world, and super-middleweight; I don't mind jumping up either."

Oliha began positively and applied pressure during the cagey opening rounds, enjoying particular success in the second as McKenna looked to establish his jab from the back foot.

McKenna, known as 'The Silencer' gradually found his rhythm, repeatedly landing his jab and uppercut while using his range effectively to avoid Oliha's heavier attacks.

The 27-year-old increasingly took control, forcing Oliha onto the ropes and landing combinations to the head and body.

Oliha continued to march forward, but McKenna's movement and defence largely nullified the Italian's pressure as he continued to land the cleaner shots.

A clash of heads left McKenna bleeding in the 11th, but he remained composed and landed several clean shots in response.

Oliha pushed forward in search of a dramatic finish in the final round, but McKenna continued to frustrate him with his jab before the final bell prompted celebrations from the Dublin crowd.

Simpson avenges only loss in Williamson rematch

In the co-main event, Cork native Callum Walsh defeated former European champion Tyler Denny by decision after a gritty 10-round battle, extending his unbeaten record to 17-0 as native fighters completed a clean sweep of wins in the Irish capital.

Joe Ward marked his return from a two-year absence with a victory over previously unbeaten Artjom Kasparian, as the Athlone boxer settled into the contest and finished strongly to earn a decision win.

In the prelims, Stevie 'The Hitman' McKenna - brother of headliner Aaron - produced an emphatic first-round knockout of Owen O'Neill, dropping the Belfast fighter with a powerful right hand just over a minute into their middleweight contest.

Derry's Connor Coyle improved to 23-0 with a unanimous decision victory over Mark Beuke, while Patrick O'Connor stopped Juan Manuel Moriel after the opening round.

title: Sabalenka and Norrie exit Canadian Open in last 16
description: World number one Aryna Sabalenka suffers a surprise defeat at the Canadian Open, while Britain's Cameron Norrie also bows out in the last 16 in Toronto.
fullText:
Women's world number one Aryna Sabalenka suffered a surprise defeat in the Canadian Open weeks before she begins her US Open title defence, while Britain's Cameron Norrie also bowed out in the last 16.

Sabalenka lost 7-6 (7-3) 4-6 6-4 to Russia's Ekaterina Alexandrova in a match lasting almost two and a half hours in Toronto.

The Belarusian recovered from a set down to force a decider, but a double fault when serving to stay in the match handed the number 16 seed victory.

It is the latest defeat in what has been a difficult summer for Sabalenka, who was knocked out in the quarter-finals and last 16 of the French Open and Wimbledon respectively.

"I just tried to play every single point as if it was the last one because with her, you don't [get] a lot of chances during the match," Alexandrova said.

"I'm super happy that I could win because after the second set, I thought [the chance] was already past me."

The Russian will face Ukraine's Elina Svitolina for a place in the semi-finals, after she defeated American eighth seed Amanda Anisimova 6-2 6-4.

Third seed Jessica Pegula suffered a first career loss to Diana Shnaider, as the 22-year-old finished both sets strongly to win 6-3 6-3.

The Russian will face Iga Swiatek in the semi-finals, after the seventh seed overcame opening set service troubles to defeat 10th seed Marta Kostyuk 3-6 6-1 6-2.

The six-time Grand Slam winner retired to the locker room after Kostyuk broke her serve four times during a shambolic a 39-minute opening set, but looked much improved when she returned.

In the men's event in Montreal, British number two Cameron Norrie spurned two set-point opportunities as he was defeated 6-2 7-6 (10-8) by 18th seed Arthur Fils.

Norrie saved three match points in the second set to force a tie-break, but the Frenchman broke his serve to win in one hour and 43 minutes.

Fils will meet Spanish teenager Rafael Jodar in the quarter-finals, after the 19-year-old upset eighth seed Jiri Lehecka 6-3 6-3.

Brandon Nakashima and Luciano Darderi also progressed to the next round with gruelling three-set victories over Arthur Rinderknech and Nuno Borges respectively.

Italian Darderi used a mid-match changeover to enjoy an espresso as he battled to a 4-6 6-3 7-5 win.

title: Trump suffers first-round defeat at China Open
description: World number one Judd Trump suffers a shock defeat by Thailand's Noppon Saengkham in the first round of the China Open.
fullText:
Judd Trump could lose his world number one ranking before the end of the month after suffering a shock defeat by Thailand's Noppon Saengkham in the first round of the China Open on Sunday.

Saengkham, ranked 45th in the world, claimed a 6-3 victory to set up a second-round meeting with either Ronnie O'Sullivan or Jackson Page.

Trump fought back from two frames down to level, before his opponent won three frames in a row to take control of the best-of-11 contest.

A match-high break of 120 put Saengkham 5-2 up, before the Thai won the final frame 78-0.

Trump, who won the China Open in 2011 and 2016, came into the event off the back of beating Kyren Wilson in the final of the invitational Shanghai Masters last week.

However, the 36-year-old has won just ranking tournaments in the past two years, the most recent of those the German Masters in February.

The China Open has returned to the World Snooker Tour calendar for the first time since 2019, and is now hosted in Taiyuan, 310 miles (500km) south west of Beijing, rather than the Chinese capital.

Trump has topped the world rankings since August 2024 but to have any chance of remaining at the summit he must win the Wuhan Open later this month and hope other results go his way.

Zhao Xintong is currently best placed to overtake Trump, with Neil Robertson and Wu Yize not far behind.

Trump was not the only seeded player to lose in the first round, as Barry Hawkins lost to Liu Hongyu, Mark Williams was defeated by Zhou Yuelong, and Ding Junhui was thrashed 6-1 by David Gilbert.

The winner of the tournament will receive prize money of £250,000, with the runner-up to bank £100,000.

title: What are your favourite new kits for the coming season?
description: BBC Sport has rounded up some of the best new kits released by clubs around the world over the summer - vote for your top 10
fullText:
As a new season draws near, football-hungry fans around the country will be tweaking their fantasy teams, making themselves experts on rumoured transfer targets and keeping eyes keenly trained on new kit releases.

It's an exciting time for collectors, whether they're looking for never-before-seen designs, classic shirts reimagined or niche releases from far-flung lands to impress their colleagues at five-a-side.

BBC Sport has rounded up a non-exhaustive list of some of the best kit releases for 2026-27 so far, ordered alphabetically.

Scroll down to the bottom of the page to vote for your top 10.

Marking 20 years since AC Milan's last Champions League title, the Rossoneri's new away shirt is modelled by legendary former player Filippo Inzaghi - who won the trophy twice with the club, including scoring a brace in the 2007 final in Athens to beat Liverpool - and current defender Davide Bartesaghi.

League One side AFC Wimbledon's away kit, in red and yellow, shares the same colour palette as the kit the team wore on the day of their promotion to the top flight for the first time ever on 3 May 1986.

Marking 20 years since the Gunners moved to Emirates Stadium, Arsenal's new home shirt has a bold red base, with white accents.

Mikel Arteta's men kick off their Premier League title defence against promoted side Coventry City on Friday 21 August.

The north London club have reprised their famous yellow for this season's third strip, with a kit reminiscent of away shirts worn by Arsenal players during the late 1980s.

Aston Villa's new home kit is an instant classic. However, the club were warned over sportswashing after revealing Visit Rwanda - the African country's tourist board - as their new front-of-shirt sponsor last month.

Atletico Madrid's new home shirt platforms the Rojiblancos' famous stripes, together with a subtle trident motif - a symbol associated with the club's fans, who gather at Madrid's Neptune Fountain to celebrate victories.

The Blaugrana have adapted their traditional stripes for this year's home kit. Hansi Flick will be aiming for a third successive La Liga title since taking over as manager in May 2024.

Adidas have gone for a retro revival with many of their kits this year and Bayern Munich's away strip sits very much in that vein - simple, clean and with the traditional trefoil logo. Vincent Kompany's team reached the Champions League final last season and have become one of the most exciting teams to watch in Europe.

Blackburn Rovers' new partnership with Umbro has been launched with an absolute stunner of a kit.

After they survived relegation from the Championship last season, manager Tony Mowbray returned to Ewood Park in June for his second spell in charge at the club.

Bournemouth struck a club-record deal with new kit supplier Hummel in May.

German manager Marco Rose will succeed Andoni Iraola at Vitality Stadium this season after the Spaniard departed having led the Cherries to their first ever European qualification.

In a commitment to affordability and sustainability, Brentford announced earlier this month that their new home kit would also be worn during the 2027-28 season.

Brighton's new home kit, with its subtle pinstripes and white neckline, draws heavily on the strip worn by the Seagulls during the 1983 FA Cup final, which they lost 4-0 in a replay against Ron Atkinson's Manchester United.

Celtic's new home shirt celebrates 60 years since the Lisbon Lions defeated Inter Milan to win the European Cup at the Estadio Nacional in Lisbon, with a commemorative badge and inscription inside the neck.

Chelsea's new home kit pays homage to their nineties 'Italian Renaissance', when Gianluca Vialli and Gianfranco Zola helped bring success to the club, including the 1997 FA Cup and 1998 League Cup.

Mexican side Club America's new home shirt is inspired by one worn during the 1998-99 season, with the club's crest blown up across the torso.

Manager Cesc Fabregas has turned Como into a serious outfit and this is a serious kit to match. The Italian side qualified for the Champions League for the first time last season and will be hoping to kick on from there.

Coventry City's new home shirt draws inspiration from the kit worn by players during the 1987 FA Cup final victory over Tottenham Hotspur.

The Sky Blues will return to the Premier League in August for the first time in 25 years after gaining promotion under manager Frank Lampard.

Scottish Championship side Dunfermline Athletic have released a shirt that harks back to the one they wore during the 1994-95 season.

The Toffees' new home shirt draws inspiration from marine flags found around the docks at the Hill Dickinson stadium.

Turkish club Fenerbahce's new away shirt is inspired by the first kit the club ever wore when they were founded in 1907.

Marking the club's centenary, Fiorentina's new home shirt features an embossed pattern inspired by the ornamental frames of Renaissance art found in the city of Florence.

Fulham's away shirt is a reinterpretation of an iconic chequered jersey worn 30 years ago during the 1996-97 season.

In 1996-97, Grimsby Town played in an away kit that was almost identical to one worn by the likes of Roberto Baggio, George Weah and Paolo Maldini at AC Milan. With Lotto returning as the League Two club's kit supplier this season, that design has been revived for a new generation of Mariners fans.

Launching their new partnership with Oxen, Hull City have released a very retro kit for the new campaign, evoking the shirts the Tigers wore during the late seventies.

Sergej Jakirovic's team will return to the Premier League for the first time in a decade this season, kicking off their campaign at home against Manchester United on Saturday 22 August.

Ipswich Town return to the Premier League this season after they were relegated at the end of the 2024-25 campaign.

The Tractor Boys' new home kit takes inspiration from the Sir Bobby Robson and Sir Alf Ramsey stands at Portman Road, with a motif copying the one that runs across the roof of the stadium.

After last season's experimental home kit, the Old Lady have returned to their traditional, thick stripes this year.

Leeds' new away shirt takes the Yorkshire rose from its club badge and repeats that motif across the base of the shirt. Blooming marvellous.

Liverpool's away shirt is inspired by the ticket stubs from European nights during the 1970s and 1980s. It also strongly brings to mind away and third kits worn during a successful period in the club's history during the late 1980s.

Liverpool's home kit for the 2026-27 campaign is a very conscious nod to the Adidas kit the Merseyside club wore between 1989-1991, during which time they won the 1989-90 First Division title under manager Sir Kenny Dalglish.

Lyon's home shirt for the new campaign pays tribute to the city, with Lyon's coat of arms silhouetted against the shirt sponsor and appearing as a subtle pattern across the stripes.

Manchester City's new home kit uses a sky blue gradient, with a print inside the neck, which reads, "Not Your Typical City". Following the departure of Pep Guardiola though, will it be typical City under new manager Enzo Maresca?

Manchester United's new away shirt is inspired by the Red Devils' 1988-90 third kit, which was only worn in three matches. The club have a history of success in blue however, having won both the 1968 European Cup final and 2017 Europa League final wearing blue kits.

Manchester United's new home kit, with its flat-knit striped collar and cuffs, is inspired by Red Devils kits from the late seventies.

To celebrate 150 years since they were founded, Championship club Middlesbrough have released this bold red and gold kit, with a special anniversary club badge displayed front and centre.

Napoli celebrate their founding in 1926 with this special kit in 'centenary blue', featuring a 100-year anniversary logo on the club badge.

Napoli's third kit evokes designs famously worn during the 1986-87 and 1988-90 seasons, when a certain Diego Maradona inspired the club to two Serie A titles.

Newcastle's new home kit uses what's been described as a 'disrupted stripe'. Just don't say it looks like a barcode. The Magpies are entering a new era this season after the shock departure of manager Eddie Howe.

French side Nice have released this classic home shirt and it is, dare we say, rather nice.

Nice's away shirt is another contender for kit of the season with its simple, but effective colour palette, classic fold-over collar and piping down the sleeves.

Nottingham Forest's home shirt is inspired by the mist that rolls in from the River Trent.

Oxford United teamed up with local street artist and lifelong U's supporter Andrew Manson to design this season's kit, along with a bespoke piece of artwork.

The European champions haven't tried to reinvent the wheel with this kit, but it oozes class. Can anyone stop Luis Enrique's side from winning a third successive Champions League trophy?

Primeira Liga champions Porto have released an away kit in gorgeous ruby - inspired by the port produced in the region as well as the River Douro.

Rangers' new home shirt is a classy affair. The Glasgow club will hope to exorcise the disappointment of last season's third-place finish under new manager Derek McInnes.

The stripes are narrower and there are interwoven diagonal lines, but this is still very definitely a Real Betis shirt - one of the most recognisable designs in European football.

Real Madrid have released their new away kit in a gorgeous, deep green, reminiscent of their 2012-13 third kit.

To celebrate their 100-year anniversary, La Liga club Real Oviedo have released a kit worth waiting a century for.

La Liga 2 side Real Valladolid's home shirt uses the club's traditional stripes, with a silhouette showing the Province of Valladolid stitched into the kit.

Sampdoria's home kit will remind fans of a certain vintage of Saturdays and Sundays spent watching David Platt represent the Serie A side on Channel 4's Football Italia.

To celebrate the club's 80-year anniversary, the shirt comes with a subtle anniversary logo embossed across the chest.

Sheffield United's away kit revives a classic style worn by the Blades during the 1975-76 season.

That campaign ended in relegation from the First Division for the Yorkshire club, but it's an iconic design nonetheless.

Ligue 1 side Strasbourg have joined the nineties revival. Their new away kit uses diamond graphics synonymous with Adidas kits from that decade, including the strips worn by the French side themselves between 1994-96.

In one of the more unexpected launches this summer, Sunderland have collaborated with the Elvis Presley estate to release this striking kit in a colourway synonymous with the King's early years in Louisiana.

Elvis' 'Can't Help Falling in Love' has been a matchday anthem for the North East club since the late seventies.

For their new home shirt, the Black Cats have drawn inspiration from the shirt worn by players during the club's first FA Cup victory at Wembley over Preston North End in 1937. A jacquard 'S' in the style of the handles of the FA Cup trophy is repeated across the base of the jersey.

After recording their highest ever WSL points total last season, Spurs are looking towards a bright future with big ambitions in the transfer market. Meanwhile, new manger Roberto de Zerbi is hoping to drag the men's side up from the depths.

To dare is to do and this kit is nothing if not daring.

Serie A club Venezia have released some of the most sought-after kits of recent years and this season's home shirt is sure to be no exception.

Wrexham's new home shirt pays tribute to their stadium, the Racecourse Ground, with a pattern reflecting the old Kop's barriers embossed into the weave of the fabric. The stand was demolished in 2023 to make way for redevelopment.
