title: Unmasking London City's Spanish superstar
description: Alexia Putellas' arrival at London City Lionesses was the biggest transfer in WSL history - but who is the person behind the global stardom?
fullText:
There is not a single empty seat as Alexia Putellas walks into a room at a hotel in Maidstone ready to speak to the English media for the first time.

"Woah," the two-time Ballon d'Or winner says as she opens the door and sees all the journalists looking in her direction, eager to finally meet her.

You would think that somebody who is referred to as 'La Reina' - the queen - in Spain is used to that kind of attention.

She is considered one of the greatest players of her generation, captained Barcelona to a fourth Women's Champions League title in May and is a World Cup winner with Spain.

But Putellas, who signed for London City Lionesses this summer in what is being touted as the biggest signing in WSL history, is embarking on a different journey with her new club that brings all the stresses and uncertainties anyone would face.

She sat down with the BBC's Women's Football Weekly podcast and addressed media in a press conference that helped unmask the global superstar.

From Barcelona to Bromley: Inside Putellas' move to LCL

Putellas was born in a municipality of Catalonia called Mollet del Valles in the province of Barcelona, and regularly watched games at Nou Camp as a child.

Former Spain and Barcelona star Andres Iniesta was an inspiration to her, while she has also named Brazilian duo Rivaldo and Ronaldinho as players she idolised.

Putellas attended summer football camps ran by Xavi and played for local side CE Sabadell as a child.

She spent a year at La Masia, Barcelona's famous youth academy, but had to leave when her girls team was disbanded.

After spells at Espanyol and Levante, she eventually returned to Barca in 2012 - the start of an incredible 14-year career with her childhood club.

"In Spain, football is the typical sport. When I was young, [it was] not for women, but fortunately, nowadays it is," said Putellas.

"I just had the ball at my feet and I was playing all the time - in the park, in the streets, sometimes at home.

"For me, it was normal because in my house Barca games were always on the TV. I started by watching games and then suddenly, I had the ball all day."

The 32-year-old went on to win 38 trophies with Barcelona, including 10 league titles and four European cups.

She was awarded back-to-back Ballon d'Or crowns in 2021 and 2022 and is favourite to win it again this year.

Internationally, she helped Spain win the 2023 World Cup and finish runners-up at Euro 2025.

But Putellas is not done. When asked if she can still get better, she laughed and said: "Yeah, of course. Always. Day after day, I want to learn things.

"That's the way I see this job. Just keep going, never stop and be as good as I can."

She described the journey she has embarked on at London City Lionesses as one that can help her "find where my limits are" as a footballer.

Putellas is enjoying pre-season but her focus never fully switches off.

"It's all about Manchester United," she says as she looks ahead to London City's season opener on 4 September (19:00 BST).

She has given up Champions League football to join London City, an independent women's-only club in its infancy. Will she need to adapt her mindset?

"Both can live together, my mentality and the moment of the project. I'm going to bring to the project whatever it needs from me," she added.

"I'm 100% committed. I'm hungry to win, I'm hungry to be better day after day and to fight with my team-mates for the victory."

Her competitiveness shines through in every conversation.

She is handed a present - a game based on the London underground - by BBC Sport.

"Oh yes, I will play with Freya Godfrey, then I can win. I will tell her that," she jokes.

That winning mentality has never changed - but she gained a new perspective when an anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury ruled her out of Euro 2022 on the eve of the tournament.

"Since the ACL injury, I enjoy everything. It's not enjoying just having fun, it's about learning something, and then I enjoy learning that thing," she added.

"I'm just a person who loves what she does. I love competition, I love football, I love training, I love to improve.

"I'm just always looking forward to better things and that's why I'm here too, because I always need to be moving as a person and a player."

Putellas is still learning the English language. She reminds journalists of that when she tries to breakdown the WSL's tactics.

"Sorry guys, I'm learning football language. This press conference maybe came early!" she jokes.

Her best friend and team mate Jana Fernandez will likely help her learn quickly, as well as several other Spaniards, including summer signing Mapi Leon from Barcelona.

But she has a better grasp of English than she realises and it is clear by the way she talks that her footballing brain is unique.

Her manager Eder Maestre says Putellas is like a secondary coach on the training pitch and has the ability to conduct the way the team plays.

"In my opinion, if I give you a pass without speaking, you have information. That's one thing I learned in Barcelona," she told the BBC.

"Maybe I am giving you that pass because I want them to receive a message like 'we go' or 'we stay.' If it's a stronger pass, it's for them to control or I want them to switch the game or whatever - it's just football language.

"Maybe I improved that in Barcelona because of the style of play. The best drills I ever trained in is about understanding what's happening in the game.

"If you understand what's happening in the game, you will get one step ahead of the opponents. When I'm training, I try to understand the way we want to play."

Putellas' fame is widespread and her grandeur was epitomised by her London City unveiling alongside billionaire owner Michele Kang in New York.

There was an emotional outpouring at her Barca departure on social media and she has 3.4m followers on Instagram.

A mural of Putellas dressed as a superhero was painted in her hometown and Nike gifted her a custom gold crown following her second Ballon d'Or victory.

"I try to not think about it, and just be like, I don't know if the word is normal, but just be me. For me, it's normal to be me," said Putellas.

She admitted walking into her first English press conference was "a little scary" and she does not generally enjoy being the centre of attention.

Her favourite part of the media day, she joked, was getting away from the cameras.

Even in the dressing room, where she is no doubt idolised by those around her, she says having former team-mates like Leon there "makes her feel more confident".

But despite the shyness, Putellas does not look out of place in the limelight. She has an obvious aura and instantly eases apprehension with humour.

In an exchange about her passing on her crown at Barcelona she quickly interjects: "No, I didn't have a crown! It's just media stuff!"

She adds: "I was just like another team-mate and so I feel like that, even if they call me 'La Reina.'

"I don't think anybody else needs to imagine 'I have a crown' and all of this because they are so good, they don't need anything from me.

"I just hope I left the team in a better position than when I started. That would make me feel so good and I enjoyed playing with them - I hope they enjoyed it as well."

Putellas' first few weeks at London City have been full of the challenges that most normal people experience - searching for a house, learning to drive in London, adapting to a new culture and developing her English.

"I have been looking for an apartment. [It's] not cheap. Well, in Barcelona, it's not cheap as well!" she said.

"Looking for where I have to go for shopping, just normal things that in Barcelona, of course, I knew. Now, here, everything is new. There's a lot of traffic here."

She has had family over to visit and has created a list of things to do in London with best friend and team-mate Fernandez.

Putellas was hoping to have dinner with England international and ex-Barcelona team-mate Keira Walsh last week but it had to be postponed.

Her friends in the WSL did give Putellas a warm welcome though...

"Well, some of them told me that it's a hard league and they're going to kick me! But no problem, I'm ready for that. No, I'm just joking...

"[They said] just enjoy the league because the games are crazy and even if you go to an away game, it's something different, something special."

Most of all, Putellas is learning to adapt to the English way of life.

She has tried a full English breakfast - but is not a fan of baked beans - and her TikTok algorithm is already throwing up typical conversational words like "innit".

"I tried an English breakfast. It's quite different from Spain. [I didn't like] the beans, but the sausages and eggs... It was fine," she joked.

"For Spanish people it's weird. Normally, we [have beans] with dinner or lunch, but not for breakfast. I don't know English culture yet!

"The weather is not bad now but I say that and people tell me, 'okay, wait for October and November.'"

But while Putellas is still adapting to life in England, it is clear she is ready to perform for London City Lionesses in September.

Her debut is likely to attract widespread attention and she hopes to embrace the occasion - after all, this is the challenge she craved.

fullText:
While the New York Yankees remain a very competitive team in the American League, they have been trying to stay afloat despite three injuries to their offensive core.

Aaron Judge, Giancarlo Stanton, and Cody Bellinger remain out due to injury. Despite their absence, the Yankees have found ways to win baseball games.

Throughout their last eight games, New York has gone 5-3. It isn't ideal, but the Yankees are staying afloat enough to allow their stars to get healthy. The hope is that they can return at some point down the final stretch of the regular season heading into the playoffs.

On Saturday, August 8, New York revealed a new update about Stanton. He hasn't played a game since April 24 when he went down with a calf injury.

Aaron Boone, the Yankees' manager, revealed some new details about Stanton. His latest update provides some optimism about a potential return sooner rather than later.

He stated that Stanton jogged in the outfield on Friday and "started the introduction to some bases." Boone also said that "I expect him back here at some point. He'll be in there when the time's right."

Stanton is still a very feared player at the plate when healthy. He may be 36 years old now, but he's still capable of taking baseballs out of the park.

Prior to the injury, Stanton played in just 24 games. He hit three home runs to go along with 14 RBI and a slash line of .256/.302/.422. Adding his production back into the lineup would be a big step towards legitimate World Series contention for New York.

Fans across the baseball world were quick to make their comments heard on social media.

"Unbelievable how this dude can barely move every season. Was on a massive hall of fame trajectory," one fan wrote.

Another chimed in, "Imagine being an MLB player and being introduced to touching a base again due to a strained calf."

"I can't wait for this dead weight to no longer be a Yankee. All time bad acquisition. The NTC should never happen again for any contract," a third fan commented.

Yet another fan said, "Honestly these updates are ridiculous and the whole Stanton situation is absurd."

"Have this man strap up for the Old Timers game at this point," another comment read.

Needless to say, fans are frustrated with how much time Stanton has missed. At 36, recovering from an injury gets a bit more difficult. Hopefully, more good news will be coming regarding the slugger in the near future.

fullText:
Barcelona are currently involved in two of the most talked about transfer sagas in European football right now in Rodri and Julian Alvarez.

Rodri, in particular, has generated a lot of buzz in recent days after the midfielder chose to join Barcelona ahead of a move to Real Madrid.

Barcelona, though, must reach an agreement with Manchester City if they are to get their hands on the Spanish World Cup winner.

Rodri is keen on joining Barcelona. (Photo by Molly Darlington/Getty Images)

According to Diario SPORT, there is total optimism within Barcelona regarding their chances of signing Rodri, with the club now treating the midfielder as their absolute priority.

The Catalans have already presented an improved offer to Manchester City, having realised their initial proposal of €45 million plus €5 million in variables fell well short of the English club's demands.

The report cites sources within the club insist they are on the right track, with one claiming the most difficult steps have already been taken and that it is now simply a case of finishing the job.

The most significant of those steps, in Barcelona's eyes, has been securing the player's desire to join.

Rodri is understood to have already informed City directly that he wants to move to Barcelona, a crucial development that the club insist eliminates the risk of any late change of heart or rival hijack.

Barcelona are not underestimating Man City's negotiating position. (Photo by Annabel Lee-Ellis/Getty Images)

Despite the confidence, Barcelona are under no illusions about the challenge that lies ahead.

Rodri still belongs to City, and the Premier League champions hold the final say on any fee.

Barcelona are aware they cannot underestimate City's negotiating position, particularly given the initial bid never stood a realistic chance of getting the deal done.

The next offer is expected to move considerably closer to City's valuation, and Barcelona accept they will have to make a significant financial effort to turn their current optimism into a concrete agreement.

Still, the belief internally is that Rodri's determination to join will ultimately help bridge the gap.

For now, then, Barcelona wait, hopeful that one of the summer's most ambitious operations can be completed.

title: Team USA dominates sprints and hurdles at World U20 Championships
description: Tate Taylor and Mia Maxwell made history as the first athletes from one country to sweep 100- and 200-meter World U20 gold.
fullText:
Tate Taylor and Mia Maxwell made history Aug. 8, becoming the first athletes from the same country to sweep the 100- and 200-meter titles at the World Athletics U20 Championships track and field meet.

The two sprinters from Texas were adorned in gold for the second time in the last three days as they each won their respective 200 finals Saturday during the fourth day of the five-day meet at Hayward Field. Both won their 100 golds on Thursday.

"More to come, better to come," Maxwell said. "This is just the beginning of what me and Tate and all the Americans' future in the sport is, so I'm excited to see what the future holds."

Taylor won the men's 200 in a meet-record 19.83 seconds, with silver going to fellow American Blake Hamilton (20.31) and bronze going to Jayden Green (20.55) of Barbados.

"To go out there and execute the way I wanted to, felt pretty good," Taylor said.

A second-place finish capped a surprisingly successful track season for Hamilton, who will soon be joining Southern California's football team for fall camp as a wide receiver.

"I mean, this silver means everything," Hamilton said. "(Going from) four months ago not really thinking about track to becoming No. 2 in the world is really big."

Maxwell won the women's 200 in a personal-record 22.37, with world season-leading Shanoya Douglas of Jamaica earning silver in 22.68 and Mia's twin sister Mariah Maxwell getting the bronze in 22.77.

"The 200 is a little bit out of my comfort zone since I'm a little bit used to running the 100 more," Mia Maxwell said. "But coming into the 200, I definitely had to come in with a different mindset and not get too comfortable off my win in the 100. I'm glad that I executed everything well. ... I'm really tired."

"Go Dawgs!" Madeline Cooper shouted with a big smile and a gold medal dangling around her neck.

It indeed was quite the night in the hurdles for the Georgia track team.

Cooper and Bulldog teammate Le'Ezra Brown swept the women's 100 and men's 110 hurdles, respectively, with Brown also tying the world U20 record.

"It's crazy," Brown beamed. "I didn't know it was gonna be that fast."

Brown finished in 12.72, comfortably ahead of silver medalist Jeremy Koga (12.97) of Japan and fellow Team USA member Zacchaeus Brocks, who equaled his PR at 12.98 for bronze.

"I knew I could do it," Brown said. " I didn't want to say it in an interview because I wanted to stay humble, but in my mind I was like, ' I'm gonna go get it.' I didn't have a great a start and I was like oh my God they're gone, but my top end is crazy, as you see."

Brown's victory came not long after Cooper schooled the women's field with her win in 12.91.

"Man, we've been talking about this since after nationals and we did it," said Brown, who was a freshman last season with Cooper. "I can't wait to see her. We probably gonna scream, yell, it don't matter. I'm proud of her."

Cooper's winning time equaled her world U20 lead. South Africa's Tumi Rankgopa was second in 12.96 and Jamaica's Tiana Marshall set a PR with her bronze-medal finish in 12.97.

"I just really had to be like, you know what, I'm the world lead, I have to trust mt abilities," Cooper said. "I know what I can do. I just ran out there. I just ran like it was a regular race. I just forgot about all the cameras, forgot about all the people here, all the pressure, and I just let it all go."

Men's 800 final: Imad Bouchajda of Morocco shot to the front with 200 to go and held on to win gold in 1:44.64. Austrailia's Daniel Williams was second in 1:45.36 and Spain's Alejandro Rios third in a PR 1:46.25.

Women's 3,000 final: Ethiopia's Yordanos Tsigab and Shito Gumi won gold and silver, respectively. Tsigab crossed in a PR 8:43.95 and Gumi in 8:45.06. The bronze went to Uganda's Charity Cherop, the 3,000 gold medalist from Wednesday.

Women's 800 final: Poland's Ziva Remic and Greece's Ioulianna Roussou ran side-by-side down the homestretch with Remic winning by a step at the finish line in 2:03.03 to 2:03.08. Great Britain's Shaikira King took bronze in 2:03.52.

Men's long jump final: Daniele Leonardop Inzoli won gold with a mark of 26 feet, 1¾ inches, but Australian Mason McGroder made him sweat when he went a PR 26-1½ on his final jump to claim silver. India's Shahnavaz Khan was third at 25-8¾.

Men's high jump final: All three medalists cleared the same height (7-3) but it was Algeria's Younes Ayachi with the fewest misses en route to a gold medal. India's Basant claimed the silver and Great Britain's Otis Poole earned the bronze.

Women's pole vault final:  Nicole Krutilova was the winner with a clearance of 14-7¼. Ukraine's Olha Belchenko cleared 14-5¼ to win silver and American Kylie Neira cleared 14-3¼ to win bronze.

Decathlon final: Sweden's Liam Belo Da Silva took the title with an 8,112-point performance. Mikai Snoek of the Netherlands was second with a PR 7,887 points and Adam Julis of Czechia was third with a PR 7,877 points.

Mixed 4x100 relay final: Italy won the gold medal with a time of 41.21 and Great Britain's Sophie Thomas outleaned American Ava Kitchings in a photo finish for silver, 41.38 to 41.39.

Men's discus prelims: Incoming Oregon freshman and reigning U.S. U20 champion Simon Rosselli advanced to Sunday's final with mark of 199-7 on his one and only attempt.

Women's 400 hurdle semifinals: U.S. U20 champion Natalie Dumas tripped over a hurdle and crashed as the race was entering the homestretch. She still finished the race but was ninth in her heat in 1:11.76. One of two captains for Team USA, Dumas won gold in the mixed 4x400 relay earlier this week.

title: Fermin Lopez talks Rodri, Ferran, Araujo exit and more – “It’s a shame since he was a captain”
description: Fermin Lopez made his long-awaited pre-season return this summer after overcoming the fractured fifth metatarsal that cost him a place at the World Cup.The midfielder featured in Barcelona’s triangu...
fullText:
Fermin Lopez made his long-awaited pre-season return this summer after overcoming the fractured fifth metatarsal that cost him a place at the World Cup.

The midfielder featured in Barcelona's triangular tournament in Udine, where the Catalans beat Nottingham Forest before losing to hosts Udinese, and afterwards spoke to the media on a range of topics.

Araujo is set to join Liverpool. (Photo by Lars Baron/Getty Images)

One of the main subjects was the departure of Ronald Araujo, who is closing in on a loan move to Liverpool.

Fermin admitted he was sad to see a teammate and captain leave, but wished him well.

"He has come to say goodbye. It's a shame, because he's a captain and I have a good relationship with him. He has decided to continue growing and hopefully he will return next season," said Fermin (h/t Diario SPORT).

The Andalusian was also asked about Ferran Torres and potential new arrival Rodri, though he insisted he did not have much information.

On Ferran's possible exit, Fermin said: "I don't want to go into that, because I don't have the necessary information. He is a good companion and a friend; I hope he decides what's best for him."

Fermin is gearing up for an important season ahead. (Photo by David Ramos/Getty Images)

He adopted a similar stance regarding Rodri, who has reportedly chosen Barcelona after his MVP-winning World Cup.

"Rodri is a great player, but he is not at the club. Whatever Deco and the sporting management decide will be fine and, if it has to happen, it will happen," he added.

Fermin, who won a decisive penalty against Nottingham Forest before being rested against Udinese, admitted he is still building up his sharpness after a difficult summer.

"Good. I still have to get into the rhythm, but I felt good. I wanted to play. It's been a very hard summer, but I'm already well and looking forward to this season," he said.

One would expect Fermin to play a key role for Barcelona next season as they look to replace the productivity of Robert Lewandowski and possibly Ferran Torres.

title: Wales must learn from Bosnia loss in Euros bid - Rush
description: Ian Rush says reaching Euro 2028 is a must for Wales as they bid to put their 2026 World Cup qualifying heartbreak behind them.
fullText:
Ian Rush believes Wales must learn from their painful World Cup play-off semi-final defeat by Bosnia and Herzegovina as they bid to qualify for Euro 2028.

The Red Dragons are winless in four matches so far this year and failed to qualify for the summer global showpiece in the USA, Canada and Mexico following their penalty shootout loss to Sergej Barbarez's side in March.

Their task is set to get tougher over the remainder of 2026 as Wales take on Portugal, Norway and Denmark in Nations League A.

But Wales legend Rush believes Craig Bellamy - who came close to leaving the Football Association of Wales to become Burnley boss earlier this summer - has the talent to deliver success with the national side.

"We have to be looking at qualifying [for Euro 2028], it's as simple as that," said Rush.

"Against Bosnia and Herzegovina, we should have won that. They beat Italy as well.

"The Euros are going to be in this country, so we need Wales to be in there."

The former Liverpool striker added: "I speak to Craig quite a lot.

"He's very, very good, so I'm looking forward to a good season and some good rounds from them because it's going to be difficult, looking at Norway, Denmark and Portugal."

Rush urges Liverpool to give Iraola time to succeed

The summer that changed Welsh football

A number of Welsh players have secured moves during the summer going into the 2026-27 season.

Goalkeeper Karl Darlow left Leeds United to join Manchester United while Harry Wilson, arguably the star performer of the Bellamy era, moved from Fulham to Leeds.

Liverpool youngster Lewis Koumas, who scored his first international goal against Ghana in June, is also expected to secure another loan switch away from Anfield having had spells with Birmingham City and Hull City last season.

"I've seen Lewis quite a lot in pre-season, he looks very, very good," said Rush, who scored 28 times in 73 appearances for his country.

"Harry Wilson, he came on in the second half, he was a major influence for Leeds in beating Liverpool.

"We're looking forward, but we've got to keep it as a team, it's up to them to do that, but I can see us doing alright."

Wales start their Nations League campaign against Portugal in Lisbon on 24 September and face Denmark in Copenhagen three days later.

Bellamy's side then host Norway and Denmark at Cardiff City Stadium in October.

The final two matches of the campaign take place in November with Wales travelling to Norway before hosting Portugal.

title: He's been frozen on Everest for 30 years, now 'Green Boots' may finally be coming home
description: For decades, an Indian man's lime shoes have been a grim trail marker for many climbing the world's highest peak.
fullText:
For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit.

The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since.

Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body – arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain.

Warning: This story contains a picture of a dead body.

They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home.

"On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC.

"When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'"

The night before he left to be part of a historic Indian expedition on Everest, Morup sat with his wife at his home in Ladakh, an Indian-administered territory in another part of the Himalayas.

He made her a promise: that he would come back a hero and make his country proud.

"He asked me to take care of the kids and come to the airport to greet him on his return," Konchak Yangskit told the BBC at her home.

A lance naik, or lance corporal, in the Indo Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), the force guarding much of India's border with China, 48-year-old Morup was no stranger to Himalayan trekking.

But Yangskit says she had a strange sense of foreboding that night: "I wondered if I was ever going to see him again."

Morup was one of six climbers on the ITBP expedition attempting to reach the top of Everest – which lies on the border between Nepal and the Chinese-governed territory of Tibet.

Most climbers choose to ascend from the Nepalese side, but Morup's crew wanted to write their names into the history books as the first Indian expedition to do it from the treacherous Chinese side.

Three out of six members of the expedition turned back due to a snowstorm, but Morup and two others - Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor – kept struggling, all the way up to the 8,849m summit.

Disaster, a blizzard, struck as they descended and killed all three.

Like many of the more than 300 people who have died in the Everest region since records began a century ago, their bodies remain on the mountain.

Two have never been found, but the third body - that of "Green Boots" - has been lying frozen in the snow for three decades at an altitude of 8,500 metres.

For years, it was assumed that "Green Boots" was another member of the expedition, Tsewang Paljor.

But testimony from surviving members of the 1996 expedition and the location of the last radio contact with the climbers have now led authorities to believe the remains belong to Morup.

An ITBP official, speaking anonymously because he is not authorised to speak to the media, told BBC News Hindi that Morup's clothes and climbing gear helped officials identify the body in recent years.

Since then, they've been plotting how to get their comrade home so they can confirm his identity beyond doubt through DNA testing and offer his family a semblance of closure.

"We never forgot him. It was only a matter of time," the ITBP official said.

Retrieving those who have died on the mountain is a dangerous, gruelling task, and, up until the past decade, very rare.

Many of the bodies, like Morup's, are in what climbers call Everest's death zone – where temperatures can plunge to -40C and oxygen levels are about a third of those at sea level.

"The weather and snow conditions are going to be crucial," said Tshiring Jangbu Sherpa, a prominent Nepalese mountaineer who has taken part in other recovery missions.

"The north side has fewer crevasses, but it is riskier. If something bad happens from the Nepalese side, you get quickly evacuated by helicopter. But there is no such system from the Chinese side," he told BBC Hindi.

The Chinese side of the peak – where Green Boots' body is – is steeper and doesn't have the same support structures as the southern slope, which is another complicating factor, Sherpa sources have told BBC News Nepali.

"It's really tough to get that body down even in popular spring season, let alone the autumn [which has more unpredictable weather]. That's the simple reason it is still there for so many years," mountaineering guide Pemba Ongchu Sherpa said.

"There would need to be 10 to 12 climbers who are capable of making summits, just to fix [support] ropes to reach that point."

Green Boots will also have to be physically carried down to an altitude where it can be collected by a helicopter, or possibly yaks, and transported back to an airport – a job which also requires huge manpower.

Sherpas say bodies shrouded in iced-up climbing gear often weigh several times the average man and are frequently frozen into awkward positions, making bringing them down the challenging terrain even more treacherous. The remains may also begin defrosting and decomposing once they reach lower altitudes.

The start of the descent with the body would be the most difficult, Indian climber Kuntal Joisher told BBC Nepali.

"It's going to be very, very risky endeavour. It's extremely steep ground with lots of rock. Logistically, this [first] 1000m is going to be a humungous challenge."

"The main thing is to not put Sherpa lives at risk for a dead body."

All of this makes for a hugely expensive recovery mission – experts say even the most straightforward ones cost between $40,000 and $80,000, a sum beyond the means of most families.

It is more common for local teams to move people who have died out of view on the mountain: like explorer Francys Arsentiev, dubbed the Sleeping Beauty of Everest, who in 2007 was moved to a more private final resting place on Everest almost a decade after she died.

But the ITBP – which is funding the recovery operation – wants Morup's body to be returned by September, and is looking for mountain rescue Sherpa groups who could do the job.

Once returned to India, the body will undergo DNA testing and, if confirmed to be Morup, his remains will be given back to his family.

For years, Morup's family back in Ladakh have struggled to come to terms with his disappearance.

Now around 75, Yangskit struggles to recall even the day she was married. But the days after the tragedy remain etched in her mind.

"I only knew there was a storm on the mountain. Even though we organised cremation prayers at home, my heart refused to believe he had died," she says with tears rolling down her face.

"I didn't see his dead body, so it was difficult for me to believe it."

All that remains of Morup today are his medals and trophies, a couple of old photos from his mountain adventures – and, most importantly, a certificate from the Chinese government which states that at 17:30 on 10 May 1996, Morup reached the top of Everest.

If the recovery mission is successful, Morup's son Punchok Dorjai told the BBC that the family would hold a funeral for him near the Martyrs Park in Ladakh's capital Leh.

"My father gave his life for the country and he should be remembered as a martyr," Dorjai said, adding that his teammates who perished deserve the same title.

The family will also proudly save a symbol of Morup's legacy at their home, to go alongside his summit certification, he said: "We are planning to keep the Green Boots."

Additional reporting by Pradeep Bashyal, BBC News Nepali

title: Google DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI role
description:

When Sir Demis Hassabis said AI had brought the world to a “pivotal moment in human history” last month, he knew another big change was imminent.
This shift was closer to home. The Nobel prize-winning head of Google DeepMind, Google’s AI unit, announced this week he was relinquishing his day-to-day duties as chief executive and becoming chair. He is also taking on the role of chief scientist at DeepMind’s parent, Alphabet.

fullText:
Observers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken over

When Sir Demis Hassabis said AI had brought the world to a “pivotal moment in human history” last month, he knew another big change was imminent.

This shift was closer to home. The Nobel prize-winning head of Google DeepMind, Google’s AI unit, announced this week he was relinquishing his day-to-day duties as chief executive and becoming chair. He is also taking on the role of chief scientist at DeepMind’s parent, Alphabet.

Hassabis and DeepMind have been key players in AI’s breakthrough era. The 50-year-old co-founded DeepMind and sold it to Google in 2014, which gave him the resources to oversee a number of advances.

These included building the AlphaGo system that mastered the Chinese board game Go and developing AlphaFold, a programme that predicts the 3D structure of proteins. The latter resulted in Hassabis being jointly awarded the 2024 Nobel prize in chemistry.

A former Google executive said the leadership overhaul showed London-based DeepMind being brought firmly into the orbit of its parent in Mountain View, California. DeepMind will now be run by Hassabis’s longstanding colleague, the US-based Koray Kavukcuoglu, who will take the non-CEO role of senior vice-president of DeepMind.

“The era of DeepMind as an independent actor is over and the obvious sign of that is you have gone from a charismatic founder-leader to appointing Koray in a non-CEO leadership role. Koray is a technical character, not an inspirational figure like Demis,” said the former executive.

The ex-Google employee added that it would be “galling” for Google and Hassabis that the latest iterations of Google’s flagship AI model series, Gemini, have lost ground to rival models developed by its US rivals Anthropic and OpenAI.

Hassabis has said he was looking forward to focusing more on the “big picture” for AI and believed he was handing over operational management of a unit that was well placed for the competitive battles ahead.

Internally, DeepMind is a workplace where there have been political tensions. Employees who spoke to the Guardian said there was internal disquiet over the company’s work with the Pentagon. Earlier this year, a former Google DeepMind employee launched a legal challenge against Google, claiming they were unfairly dismissed for their views on Gaza.

That employee was involved in unionisation efforts at Google DeepMind, which have taken place against a backdrop of concern that Google’s AI could assist militaries, including the Israel Defense Forces. Another Google DeepMind employee resigned from the company in mid-July, citing Google’s work with the Pentagon and the US Department of Homeland Security.

One said to the Guardian that Hassabis’s departure was the “end of an era”.

“Now the person we were supposed to trust to get the right outcomes for humanity has stepped away,” they said. Google DeepMind “has become just another subdivision of Google”, they added.

Rosa Curling, the executive director of Foxglove, a campaign group that supported the Google DeepMind employee in their legal challenge, said: “The departure of the co-founder of a company that once prided itself on its ethical credentials is likely to cause further concern among its frontier AI staff about how their work will end up being used in the real world.”

Google has said it is committed to the “private and public sector consensus” that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without “appropriate human oversight”. While Google has declined a voluntary union recognition agreement in London, it has said it valued “the constructive and direct dialogue that we have with our employees about building a positive and successful workplace”.

On the commercial side, a new cutting-edge model, Gemini 3.5 Pro, has yet to be released amid reports it has been delayed owing to attempts to improve its code-writing abilities – a core part of the appeal of Anthropic and OpenAI’s best products.

Google’s two AI labs, London-based DeepMind and California-based Google Brain, were merged into Google DeepMind under Hassabis’s leadership three years ago. Control now appears to be moving back to the US, where Google’s co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly playing a bigger role in AI development.

Citing the departure of the leading AI researcher Yann LeCun from Meta and Geoffrey Hinton from Google as another example of “the end of an era in the AI ecosystem”, the former executive added: “This is very clearly a sign that the science-driven agenda of leadership in these labs has given way to cold, hard commercial reality that all of these companies want to make a return on the hundreds of billions of dollars they have invested in AI.”

The source added, however, that Google still had the benefit of being able to combine its Gemini models with an impressive suite of products, from its all-conquering search product to its cloud platform and YouTube. Thanks to its search business it also has the money to continue investing heavily in AI, having generated net income – a US measure of profit – of $132bn (£98bn) last year.

Hassabis has also taken on a more statesman-like role in recent years. The reference to a “pivotal moment” came in a blogpost in which he called for a US safety body to assess cutting-edge models, with the hope it would lead to the establishment of global standards.

The need for such a body, Hassabis argued, was pressing because the tech industry was approaching the “pivotal” point of achieving AGI, the term for a theoretical state of AI where a system can perform any human cognitive task – which also means being capable of performing white collar jobs in sectors such as law, finance and health.

A Google spokesperson said: “This is a move Demis has been thinking about for a while. He is very excited, and this will give him more time to focus on AI-driven scientific breakthroughs.” They disputed that the changes had anything to do with the performance of Gemini.

Hassabis’s move was announced alongside the departure of Jeff Dean, a veteran Google engineer and DeepMind’s chief scientist, who is leaving along with three other top researchers to form an AI startup called Discovery Loop.

According to one former Google employee, Dean’s departure could augur further personnel losses. Dean’s move also follows OpenAI’s poaching in June of Google’s Noam Shazeer, a leading figure in the field as co-author of the 2017 research paper Attention is All You Need, a crucial step in developing chatbots.

“It’s hugely problematic for Google,” said Jeremy Nixon, a former AI researcher at Google and founder of Infinity Artificial Intelligence Institute, a startup. “It’s problematic because of who Jeff will hire and because the primary reason people want to work at Google is because of him and Noam Shazeer and all these other phenomenal researchers. It’s no longer true to say that if you want to work with the greatest researchers on the planet, you go to Google DeepMind.”

Nixon added that Dean was an “angelic diplomat” who could “deal with these complex political organisations”.

Google denies it faces a post-Dean talent crisis, pointing to attrition rates for AI talent for the first half of this year being lower than they were at this time last year.

If AI is indeed facing a pivotal moment, Google has just had one.

fullText:
The mission of the Flock app is quietly subversive: to encourage users to ditch their screens and explore the wonderful world of birding

On a brilliantly bright afternoon in his gallery and studio in Bolinas, a small town on the northern California coast, Keith Hansen was putting the finishing touches on a watercolor of an almost improbably flamboyant painted bunting.

With an ultra-fine sable brush, he made a few intricate additions to the cobalt blue plumage on the bunting’s head, and, satisfied with his work, slipped the watercolor into a stout binder that every few days welcomes a new addition.

“That was number 420,” he said. Or to put it another way, just 584 to go.

Hansen, a renowned ornithological illustrator and author, has a monumental task – a hand-painted compendium of every one of the roughly 1,000 bird species ever recorded from the US and Canada, including those found in waters up to 200 miles from shore, Hawaiian birds not included. When finished, it will complete the visual backbone of an app called Flock, whose mission, compared with that of most apps, is quietly subversive.

For rather than seeking to monopolize and monetize its users’ attention, it deftly employs elements of computer gaming and social networking to draw people outward, into the world of birding, with the broader aim of cultivating a community of conservationists.

Flock was conceived and created by two of Hansen’s friends, Adam Donkin and Bob Stevenson. Both have impressive tech industry CVs. Donkin, 52, who lives not far from Hansen in Marin county’s San Geronimo valley, worked for many years as a product and user experience designer. As a lead product designer at Amazon, he led the charge on design for several models of the Kindle e-reader.

Stevenson, a 58-year-old Scotsman, lives in St Helena in the Napa valley. He founded his first company in Edinburgh at 18, and at 24, moved to California to work as an art director for Richard Branson’s Virgin Games, embarking on a decades-long career as an art or design director, or as a producer, for more than 50 video games.

Despite their disparate disciplines, the three friends are united by a shared passion for birds and birding.

Hansen fell in love with the avian world in sixth grade, when, on a walk in the Maryland woods, his brother, Rob, drew his attention to a cedar waxwing. “It’s just an exquisite bird,” Hansen recalled. He began illustrating birds during his senior year of high school, and in 1986 – after a decade and a half observing and studying birds on numerous expeditions – he settled in Bolinas, opening his gallery there in 1991.

Donkin grew up on the San Francisco peninsula and began birding at the age of four under the wing of his father’s friend Rich Stallcup, an esteemed ornithologist and birder, and a founder of the Point Reyes Bird Observatory. “He was like a nature wizard,” said Donkin. “Birds and animals would appear when you were in the field with him. He knew every bird by call and by sight.”

Donkin moved to Marin in 2012. “When I moved to Marin,” he said, “Rich introduced me to the thriving birding community here, including Keith.”

That same year, Stevenson was looking for a designer for his new company. “One of our investors recommended that we chat with this designer, Adam,” said Stevenson. “It was meant to be a quick call, but we ended up talking for over an hour. We became friends on the first call.”

In 2016, Donkin visited Stevenson at his home in the southern Marin town of Tiburon, overlooking Richardson Bay, a major habitat for migrating waterbirds. “One day Adam came round to the house,” Stevenson recalled. “I didn’t know that he was an avid birder. He turned up and said, ‘Hey, dude, you’ve got to bird! Do you have binoculars?’”

Stevenson, who had recently stepped away from his company to focus on his family, fell hard and fast for birding. He bought binoculars, scopes and cameras, began birding from his deck, and, as an outlet for his avian photography, opened his own gallery in Tiburon.

He was also struck by the ways in which birding resembled multi-player gaming, in that it involved learning new skills, a mastery curve, collecting (by way of so-called yard lists and life lists – tabulations of the bird species sighted in one’s yard, or over a lifetime), an awareness of how one is progressing relative to others, and a community which, while competitive, helps its members learn more quickly. He also recognized, at the age of 48, what he had given up by trading the beauty of the natural world for computer screens. “It was such a revelation, because going back to nature at that age, you realize what you’ve been missing.”

Shortly after, he and Donkin began discussing the idea of building an app around birding. For Donkin, his friend’s newfound passion was a catalyst. “I had the experience with Bob of turning someone on to it, and seeing what a huge impact it had on him.”

For Stevenson, the spark was a conversation with Robert Snow, the president of the Fresno Audubon Society, who said the organization was concerned about its ability to bring future generations into birding, as this was critical to perpetuating its mission of protecting birds and their habitats.

To Donkin, the path from birding to conservation is a natural progression. “Birding creates an infinite well of curiosity,” he said. “You start to notice things and think, ‘Well, how can I help?’ You might start with providing water, providing food, providing shelter. By restoring habitat in your area, you can have an impact. It could be your yard, a park in your neighborhood, sometimes ranch land, sometimes public land.”

Initially Stevenson and Donkin thought they might develop an app in partnership with Audubon, or with the Cornell Lab of Ornithology in Ithaca, New York, where they had given a presentation on the parallels between birding and gaming, with an eye towards how aspects of game design could be employed to increase engagement with the Cornell Lab’s Merlin app, which identifies birds based on their songs and calls, or images.

They ultimately decided to strike out on their own and, in 2017, set to work on Flock. Having worked on projects backed by publishers and by investors in Silicon Valley, Stevenson said they decided to fund it themselves “so we would not be bound by anyone’s rules”. They also set out to break the addictive conventions of app design. “The games industry is so comfortable making experiences that are so engaging that you can’t look away,” said Donkin, “and we were very aware of the negative aspects of social media.”

“We didn’t want to make something that got you addicted to the dopamine hit of getting a like, or followers,” Donkin continued. “We wanted to make something that was a companion to the experience of birding. In an attention-based economy, we’re going to use that same system, but we’re going to flip it. We’re not trying to get your attention on the app, we’re trying to get your attention away from your phone so that you can then turn your attention outward.”

The result is an app whose interface is refreshingly spare and minimalistic, with a tab where users can search for birds or for other users; another for recording sightings, made, perhaps with the aid of the Merlin app or an old-fashioned field guide; a leaderboard which ranks users according to the number of unique species they saw in the current month; and a community tab where users can upload photos, message one another, and congratulate other users on their sightings.

As with every detail of the app, even the way in which users cheer one another on was carefully considered. Instead of a “like” button, there is a “high-five” button. “We put ‘high five’ rather than ‘like’,” Stevenson explained, “because kids were using it, and we wanted it to be, ‘Nice job on seeing that bird!’ rather than, ‘I like you.’ We didn’t want kids to collect likes.”

They enlisted their longtime friend Hansen, whose artistic sensitivity brought a unique beauty to the app. While Stevenson coded, Donkin scanned and processed new batches of illustrations as Hansen completed them, following an algorithm that sorted the bird species in order from the most- to the least-commonly seen. Given that it can take Hansen up to four days to complete an illustration, this prioritized the birds Flock users are more likely to encounter: an American robin or a northern cardinal, for instance, rather than a Steller’s sea eagle, a huge Siberian raptor, one of which, acting on some unknown impulse in 2020, flew from northern Asia to Alaska and then Texas, before settling on the coast of Maine.

In early 2025, they released Flock on Apple’s app store. By April of that year, Flock had about 100 users. Today, although Donkin and Stevenson have not yet done anything in the way of marketing, it has on the order of 1,000. Among the recent enhancements they enjoy are uncannily realistic animations that bring Hansen’s illustrations to life. The short animations – which Stevenson created with AI, with Hansen’s guidance – give a sense of the way each particular bird moves. The formerly static white-crowned sparrow now darts its head this way and that in a most sparrow-like fashion, peering inquisitively at its viewer; the great blue heron, meanwhile, tiptoes along a sandy bank, and pausing, stealthily lowers its bill to the water’s surface, preparing to strike.

Among Flock’s growing flock is Amy Tan, the bestselling writer whose most recent work, The Backyard Bird Chronicles, grew from a series of pencil sketches, color portraits and journal notes she collected on her avian neighbors during the pandemic. A friend of Hansen’s for 10 years, and more recently of Stevenson’s, Tan logged her first sightings in the app late last summer. In an email, Tan wrote that Flock was “hands down the most beautiful bird app and the easiest one to track and share sightings of my backyard birds. With each bird I add to my daily list, I feel rewarded when its illustration suddenly comes to life. All my friends are blown away and become instant fans.”

This reporter, meanwhile, who entered his first sighting – a western gull – in Flock last spring, has found himself growing ever more attuned to the sights, sounds and habits of his feathered compatriots in San Francisco, and has recently begun shopping for a hummingbird feeder.

title: Pritchard eyes world title defence after Euro win
description: The 34-year-old from Mumbles, near Swansea will head to Amsterdam having overcome a freak pre-Europeans injury to retain his title in Italy.
fullText:
Welsh Para-rower Ben Pritchard hopes his successful European title defence can be the springboard to retaining his world title later this month.

The 34-year-old will head to Amsterdam having overcome a freak pre-event injury to beat Italian Giacomo Perini in the PR1 men's single sculls at the European Rowing Championships in Varese, Italy last weekend.

"When I landed in Italy, there was a malfunction on the hoist that got me on to the coach and the cable snapped, so it dropped me from the top of the hoist to the bottom, which obviously causes a bit of an injury, which I was managing throughout the championships," Pritchard told BBC Radio Wales Breakfast.

Pritchard, from Mumbles, Swansea, added: "I actually thought I may not have come out on top given the injury that I was coping with, but I'm glad I did. It was a great race though.

"It's probably one of the best races we've had in in a couple of years because it was neck and neck until the last 250m."

Pritchard named BBC Wales Sports Personality of the Year 2025

Pritchard, the BBC Cymru Wales Sports Personality of the Year for 2025, and his Great Britain team-mates have stayed at Varese to complete their preparations for the World Rowing Championships, that take place from 24-30 August at Amsterdam's Bosbaan venue.

"I always feel that this this camp is where we get the most speed," said Pritchard.

"We do a load of speed work in this last block now for the world championships, so I'm hoping that that'll set me in good stead for the future.

"I have just seen my competitor Erik Horrie from Australia training this morning, and he looks really fast as well. So hopefully we can get a good race but it's an outdoor sport - anything could happen.

"But it's going to be nice to be out on the Bosbaan in Amsterdam because the Welsh men's hockey team and ladies' team have got their World champs as well, so I'm going to hopefully get across and watch some of their games too."

Pritchard is one of Para-rowing's dominant forces. Since winning gold at the 2024 Paralympics he has set multiple world records in his event and added the 2025 European and world crowns to his tally.

He says he went to Italy with added desire to succeed after his Swansea coach Andrew Williams lost his father.

"It was a big one and an emotional one, but gave you the actual motivation when the going got tough in the race, that's for sure," he said.

However, Pritchard was comfortable facing and beating Perini on his home waters, saying: "I think it's more my home water than his.

"You know, we're in his home country, but as a team, we come here twice a year to train and spend two weeks of time here, so I've been coming here now for nine years.

"It feels like a home to me, and the club members know me and all that kind of stuff, so I feel that actually I had a good share of the support in the stands."

title: 'Having skill is one thing': Shikhar Dhawan drops big verdict on Vaibhav Sooryavanshi

fullText:
Former India opener Shikhar Dhawan has praised teenage batter Vaibhav Sooryavanshi, saying the youngster's fearless batting and ability to perform at such a young age make him special.

Speaking to news agency ANI, Dhawan said it is a big achievement for a 15-year-old to reach the international level and deliver consistent performances. He also pointed to Sooryavanshi's IPL displays, saying the teenager's confidence in hitting boundaries stands out.

Dhawan said talent alone is not enough, and added that having the courage and mindset to play attacking cricket at such a young age is what sets Sooryavanshi apart. He also backed the youngster to continue doing well in the years ahead.

"He is batting very superbly. And it's a very big thing that at the age of 15 or 16, reaching the international level first is a big thing in itself. Even when he was playing in the IPL. But the way he hits fours and sixes, that's a wonderful thing. Having skill is one thing, but having the heart for it, and that too at 15, is a very big thing. And I'm sure that his present is also very good and his future will also be very good," Dhawan said.

Sooryavanshi, 15, recently enjoyed a successful T20I series against Zimbabwe, scoring 151 runs in three matches to win his maiden Player of the Series award as India completed a 3-0 clean sweep.

Earlier, during the T20I series against England, Sooryavanshi became the youngest player to make his international debut for India.

His India debut came after a successful IPL 2026 season with Rajasthan Royals. He scored 776 runs at a strike rate of 237.30, including one century and five fifties. He finished as the tournament's highest run-scorer and hit a record 72 sixes.

Sooryavanshi also won the Orange Cap, Most Valuable Player, Emerging Player, Super Striker and Super Sixes awards after the season.

Earlier this year, he also impressed in the ICC Men's Under-19 Cricket World Cup, scoring 439 runs and winning the Player of the Tournament award.

title: Saudi Arabia turns to Muslim military heavyweights in landmark defense pact as Iran war closes in
description: Saudi Arabia has drawn two of the Muslim world’s most formidable military powers into its defense as the Iran war moves closer to the kingdom.
fullText:
Saudi Arabia has drawn two of the Muslim world's most formidable military powers into its defense as the Iran war moves closer to the kingdom.

Pakistan and Turkey signed a NATO-style mutual defense pact with Saudi Arabia in Mecca on Friday, consolidating their longstanding security ties into a collective-defense alliance that stipulates an attack against any of them "shall be regarded as attack on them all."

That commitment could draw Pakistan and Turkey into a war they have carefully kept at arm's length.

The official rationale for the agreement is "to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression" and further provide "for the enhancement of all aspects of defence cooperation among the three states," according to a statement released by all three countries.

More specifically, the pact gives Saudi Arabia a powerful new layer of protection beyond its longstanding security partnership with the United States amid growing regional doubts over whether Washington can still be relied upon to protect its oil-rich Gulf allies.

Turkey has the second-largest military in NATO, behind only the US, while Pakistan is the only nuclear-armed Muslim nation.

Such powerful allies strengthen Saudi deterrence and present a united Sunni-led military front against a mounting Iranian threat, though a Turkish official told CNN the agreement isn't directed against any specific actor and the Saudi foreign ministry insisted this "does not represent an effort to establish a military axis or a sectarian bloc."

Other regional countries can also join, the Turkish official added, raising the prospect of the alliance drawing in new members much like NATO.

The statement ⁠did not give specifics on the commitments each had accepted, and it is unclear how far the agreement would bind the three countries to any particular military action in each other's defence.

The pact also comes as Israel expands its military reach across the region and Riyadh's relations with the neighboring United Arab Emirates fray.

Pakistan and Turkey each share a border with Iran and both have strong reasons to prevent the conflict from spiraling. Pakistan must manage its sizeable Shiite population and its sensitive relationship with Tehran, while Turkey and Iran share concerns over Kurdish separatism despite competing elsewhere in the region.

Tehran repeatedly struck targets in Saudi Arabia during the war, including civilian infrastructure, energy facilities and US interests. Direct Iranian attacks on Saudi Arabia largely subsided after an April 8 ceasefire took hold, but Iran-backed groups in Yemen and Iraq continued targeting the kingdom.

Riyadh has been one of the war's most vocal opponents and has worked to restrain US President Donald Trump from escalating against the Islamic Republic. Yet the attacks Saudi Arabia continues to face from multiple fronts have left officials increasingly alarmed and frustrated.

A Saudi official told CNN on Thursday that the kingdom was bracing for a major, coordinated assault by Iran-backed militias in Iraq and Yemen, supported by Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. CNN has also reported that Tehran warned Gulf nations that renewed US attacks would trigger retaliation against energy or desalination facilities across the region.

The treaty signed in Mecca on Friday therefore serves as a warning to Tehran: another major attack on Saudi Arabia could invoke the pact, draw Pakistan and Turkey into the conflict and dramatically widen the war.

Reaction emerging from Tehran indicated their dissatisfaction toward the agreement, as a senior Iranian official warned that it will not guarantee Saudi Arabia's security.

"The Saudis should understand that a paper agreement with Turkey and Pakistan will not bring them security, just as decades of one-sided dependence on the Americans failed to do so," Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the Iranian parliament's National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said on X.

The agreement solidifies deepening military ties between these nations. Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed a formal mutual defense pact last September, even before Iran started directly striking Saudi sites,

CNN's Issy Ronald, Aida Karimi, Gul Tuysuz and Sophia Saifi contributed reporting.

title: Scotland beat Canada to reach World Cup Qualifier
description: Scotland hold on for a nervy nine-run victory over Candada to secure a place at next year's World Cup Qualifier after a tense tri-series match in Forfarshire.
fullText:
ICC Men's Cricket World Cup League 2 tri-series, Forthill

Scotland 281-7 (50 overs): McCreath 112; Shirzad 3-55

Canada 272 (49.2): Samra 78; McMullen 3-43

Scotland held on for a nervy nine-run victory over Candada to secure a place at next year's World Cup Qualifier after a tense ICC Cricket World Cup League 2 match in Forfarshire.

Fin McCreath's 112, his first international century, helped the hosts post 281-7 at Forthill.

Canada hit 50 inside eight overs thanks to Yuvraj Sumra (78), but they fell to 181-7 only for a partnership of 84 by Ansh Patel and captain Saad Bin Zafar to take them close to their target before George Munsey's catch secured Scotland's win with four balls remaining.

Scotland are now assured a place at next year's Qualifier as Canada cannot catch them in the League 2 standings.

It was the first game of the tri-series, which also involves the United Arab Emirates, to beat the wet weather after two washouts.

Grange batter McCreath reached his century from 135 balls in the 47th over.

title: Rashid takes six wickets as Afghanistan thrash Ireland
description: Rashid Khan takes six wickets as Afghanistan beat Ireland by 92 runs in Gary Wilson's first one-day international as head coach.
fullText:
Afghanistan 299-8 (47 overs): Zadran 84 (97); Adair 2-40

Ireland 207 all out (33.4 overs): Carmichael 62 (66); Rashid 6-34

Rashid Khan took six wickets as Afghanistan beat Ireland by 92 runs in Gary Wilson's first one-day international as head coach.

After Wednesday's opener if the five-game series was washed out without a ball bowled, a wet outfield at Bready led to a 90-minute delay and a reduction of three overs per side.

Afghanistan quickly took advantage of the short boundaries at the County Tyrone ground, with a succession of batters looking set even if it was only Ibrahim Zadran who went on to pass fifty.

His 84 helped Afghanistan post 299-8 ,but Ireland could only muster 207 as Wilson's reign started with defeat.

Cade Carmichael was Ireland's top scorer with 62, but Rashid stole the show with six wickets.

The tourists have won seven ODIs against Ireland in succession, a run that stretches back to 2019.

Ireland's first ODI with Afghanistan washed out

As has been the case throughout this home summer, Ireland's bowling options were limited through injuries.

Josh Little, Matt Hollard, Craig Young and Barry McCarthy were all enforced absentees, with Wilson's first selection showing four specialist bowlers including international debutant Byron McDonough.

There was plenty of interest to see how Jai Moondra, breakout star of June's T20 series victory over India, would fare in his one-day bow with the India-born 29-year-old's two wickets coming at a cost of 78 runs.

Among that total were nine fours and three sixes with Afghanistan plundering 32 boundaries across their innings.

Seamer Mark Adair was the pick of the bunch for Ireland, even if 14 off his final over inflated his figures to 2-40.

After he signed off from The Hundred duty with figures of 5-17 for MI London on Sunday, Ireland were left wishing Rashid had seen out the season on the franchise circuit.

Back with Afghanistan, the number one-ranked ODI bowler in the world accounted for the early wickets of Andrew Balbirnie and Harry Tector, while Azmatullah Omarzai dismissed captain Paul Stirling and Carmichael.

Rashid also removed both Curtis Campher and Ben Calitz as he finished with 6-34 from 7.4 overs..

It was a disappointing start for new head coach Wilson, but Ireland have the opportunity to bounce back in the third match of the series at Stormont on Monday.

The fixtures are preparation for the 2027 World Cup qualifiers, which are set to begin next year.

title: Politicians, private jets and power - the life of a Fifa president
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino appears to be trying to return to business as usual after the failed World Cup private investment plan - but it may not be that easy.
fullText:
Gianni Infantino stepped off a plane in Cali and was greeted on the runway by the president of the Colombian Football Federation.

Ramon Jesurun, a close ally of Infantino's, saw it as a chance to show his support, with the two men smiling in a photo opportunity for the federation's Instagram account.

Infantino had not travelled to Colombia for any run-of-the-mill meeting on Friday. He would attend the inauguration of the country's new president Abelardo de la Espriella.

Infantino was accompanied by Alejandro Dominguez, the president of South America's football governing body Conmebol, who praised both his record and the "enormously successful" 2026 World Cup, saying "we stand with Gianni".

This is the life of a Fifa president.

It involves building ties with some of the most powerful people in the world, shown by Infantino's relationship with US President Donald Trump.

Before the biggest scandal to hit his tenure - the aborted Fifa Forward Enterprise plan - Infantino was an incredibly powerful figure who appeared bulletproof.

Now, after an apology and stated desire to withstand the backlash of his plan to sell a stake in the men's World Cup to private equity firms, Infantino appears to be trying to return to business as usual.

Uefa's threat to boycott Fifa tournaments still stands. That will be tested with the Fifa Under-20 World Cup set to kick off in Poland in 29 days.

Perhaps emboldened by the support he has received from outside Europe in recent days, Infantino is not going to stand down easily.

But what exactly is the role of the Fifa president?

A cavalcade of blacked out Mercedes, flanked by police cars, rolled into the Fifa headquarters in Rabat, Morocco, earlier this week.

Infantino had summoned a select few members of the Fifa management board to discuss his plan to sell off 21% of the commercial and ticketing business to a private equity firm.

This is how the Swiss-Italian travels - in between flights on the Qatar Airways Executive jet which has been made available to him. The plane enabled him to take up to three flights a day, watching two games, throughout the 2026 World Cup.

That type of arrival does look presidential - only more like a president of a country than a sports body.

It enables him to travel the globe, visiting Fifa's official offices like Rabat, where he was based over the past week as the Fifa Forward Enterprise controversy developed.

In his role Infantino is expected to visit the 211 member nations, to see the grassroots projects Fifa has funded.

Part of his remit is to unify football, which cannot be achieved from within the Fifa headquarters in Zurich.

It requires international travel to attend confederation meetings, and the global tournaments Fifa organises. Infantino needs to build relationships with officials and politicians.

In April, before the Fifa Congress in Vancouver, local authorities rejected a request for a level-four motorcade, usually reserved for heads of state or the Pope.

New Zealand police said they had declined a similar request during the 2023 Women's World Cup.

Alongside the cavalcade of cars and the private charter flights comes a large salary, too, three times what he first earned when elected in 2016.

Infantino, who was paid about £1.3m 10 years ago, now takes home about £4m - a base salary of £2.2m plus a confirmed variable bonus payment of £1.8m.

His predecessor Sepp Blatter was paid a £2.6m package for his final year as Fifa president.

Infantino gets a 'per diem' too to cover expenses and living costs, worth £20,500 a year on top of his salary.

As the head of the most popular sport in the world, it should be expected that there is a wage to match.

Infantino would argue that by driving record revenues and funding for member associations, he has proven he is worth the salary.

Infantino's alliance with Trump seemed to have elevated his status even further.

Many in world football felt that this began to come at the expense of his responsibilities in football.

In May 2025, Infantino had been on a diplomatic tour of the Middle East with Trump and turned up two hours late for the Fifa Congress in Paraguay.

title: The Anniversaries of Hiroshima and Nagasaki Have Special Meaning in a World Out of Control
description: William D. Hartung, Mari...
fullText:
As the last US-Russia nuclear arms control treaty expires, the anniversaries of Hiroshima and Nagasaki carry renewed urgency for a world edging toward a new arms race.

This August marks yet another anniversary of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, but 2026 carries a special weight—for the first time since the Cold War, the United States has no active nuclear arms control treaty with Russia, following the expiration of the New START nuclear arms reduction agreement.

Over 80 years ago, the United States dropped two atomic bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki. The uranium bomb detonated over Hiroshima on August 6 destroyed an estimated 70 percent of the city’s buildings and roughly 140,000 lost their lives. Less than five days later, a plutonium bomb was dropped on the nearby city of Nagasaki, killing an additional 74,000 people, triggering radioactive rain, and driving ground temperatures above 4,000°C. In the years and decades that followed, the few survivors who lived faced immense health complications including leukemia, cancer, deformities, and other devastating health impacts from radiation—impacts those communities are still living with today.

New START itself can be traced back to the Soviet era, when the United States and Russia first launched the SALT negotiations that eventually produced the Treaty on Measures for the Further Reduction and Limitation of Strategic Offensive Arms: a heralded treaty, that went through multiple iterations, that many subsequently considered the last bastion constraining a renewed global nuclear arms race. That treaty expired on February 5, 2026.

In addition to the dangerous dismantling of the modest controls on nuclear escalation that had existed for decades, there has been a systematic effort to erase the devastation of the communities that have been hurt most by the development, production, and testing of nuclear weapons from our memories, and our history books. The combination of an absence of guardrails and an attempt to induce historical amnesia about the true human costs of developing and maintaining vast nuclear arsenals is a volatile mix that increases the risks that nuclear weapons might be used again, despite the lessons of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

The story of nuclear weapons is more than just the story of scientists working away in secrecy at Los Alamos, or leaders wielding nuclear threats—and, in the case of the Cuban missile crisis, bringing the world to the brink of nuclear war. It is the story of devastation, disease, and death caused by the development and deployment of those weapons, even if they are never used again in warfare. The deadly consequences of nuclear development have fallen most heavily on communities of color, from the dire health consequences of mining uranium in the Congo and the American Southwest, to the generational cancers in communities downwind from nuclear tests, from the Marshall Islands to the American West; communities of color have been disproportionately affected by nuclear testing and warfare.

These consequences did not start with the bombings in Hiroshima or Nagasaki. The testing caused a reckoning that also reached into the scientific community itself, made famous by Robert Oppenheimer’s words after the Trinity test, when he said the world would not be the same, and later invoked the line “I am become Death, the destroyer of worlds.” Historians still debate the racialized dimensions of why the bomb was used on Japan; questions of who counts as human, who is deemed worthy of safety, and how ideas of supremacy shape militarization remain unresolved eight decades later. That choice—its weight—also strained the diplomatic relationship between the United States and Japan, raising a question that still lingers: How does a nation set norms it did not itself follow?

The stories of the civilian victims of nuclear arms racing are increasingly at risk of being rewritten, sanitized, or erased from official histories altogether. The risks posed by the lack of arms control measures and the concerted effort to whitewash the dangers of possessing nuclear weapons, as well as the catastrophe that would come from using them, make nuclear use at some future date more likely. With no treaty framework in place, active global conflicts like the runaway wars in the Middle East and the ongoing war in Ukraine, and coordinated efforts to erase the history of nuclear dangers, we need to treat this anniversary as more than a commemoration or an expression of regret. We need to treat it as a turning point for humanity.

We need not just a moment of mourning but a call to chart a new path forward that recognizes the dreadful toll nuclear weapons have imposed, and takes fundamental steps toward reducing nuclear dangers once and for all. As the US has reached its 250th birthday, it is long past time for some truth-telling about communities harmed by the bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, and about countries all over the world harmed by nuclear weapons.
